0.title: Do Not Be Shaken
0.overview:
The message. Second Thessalonians steadies a frightened church. Someone had told the believers in Thessalonica that “the day of the Lord has come” (2:2), and the eager hope of the first letter had turned to alarm. Paul answers that the day has not come, that certain things must happen first, and that when it comes it will bring relief to God’s suffering people and judgment on those who afflict them. Meanwhile they are to stand firm and keep working. False teaching about the end produces disordered living; true teaching about the end produces settled, patient, working disciples. The anchor of it all is one short sentence: “But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one” (3:3).

Background: the writer. The letter comes from Paul, Silvanus and Timothy (1:1), the same three who sent the first letter. They were together in Corinth, where Paul stayed “a year and six months” (Acts 18:5, 11), so it was probably written there, about AD 50 or 51, only weeks or months after 1 Thessalonians.

Thessalonica. Thessalonica, today’s Thessaloniki in northern Greece, was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, a busy port on the Via Egnatia, the great road from Italy to the East. It was a free city with its own magistrates; the “city authorities” of Acts 17:6 were officials called politarchs, a title confirmed by inscriptions found there. Its people worshipped many gods, among them Dionysus and the Egyptian Serapis and Isis, and the city honoured Rome and its emperors as benefactors. That made the charge against the first believers dangerous: they were “acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus” (Acts 17:7), in the reign of Claudius.

Paul and the church there. Paul and Silas came on his second journey, about AD 49 or 50, and on three Sabbaths reasoned in the synagogue that the Christ had to suffer and rise. Some Jews believed, with “a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women” (Acts 17:4), but most of the church were Gentiles who had “turned to God from idols” (1 Thessalonians 1:9). A mob attacked Jason’s house, and the brothers sent Paul and Silas away by night (Acts 17:5–10). While there Paul had worked “night and day” so as to be no burden (3:8). Most members were probably working people, in a culture where the well-to-do despised manual labour and many lived as clients of richer patrons.

What prompted the letter. Three things had grown worse since the first letter. The persecution had deepened (1:4–7). Some had been alarmed by a claim, “either by a spirit or a spoken word, or a letter seeming to be from us” (2:2), that the day of the Lord had come: perhaps a supposed prophecy, perhaps a forged letter, perhaps a twisting of what Paul had written. And some would “walk in idleness, not busy at work, but busybodies” (3:11), living off others, though Paul had already told them to “work with your hands” (1 Thessalonians 4:11). Excitement about the end may have fed this, and the generosity of richer members may have made it easy.

Did Paul really write it? Many modern scholars think a later writer composed it in Paul’s name. They point to its close likeness in wording to 1 Thessalonians, its cooler tone, and what they see as a different picture of the end: in the first letter the day comes “like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2); here certain events must come first. But the church received it as Paul’s from the start: Polycarp seems to echo it, Marcion’s collection of Paul’s letters included it, and Irenaeus quotes it as his. The likeness is natural if the same men wrote again within months. The two pictures fit together: the day will surprise the unprepared, yet God has fixed what must come before it. And a forger would hardly warn against letters falsely claiming to be Paul’s (2:2) and then close with his signature, “the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine” (3:17). The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote it, partly to correct a misreading of his first letter.

How the letter makes its case. Two convictions frame the letter. Chapter 1 sets out the righteous judgment of God: to a church under persecution, wrong will not go unanswered: God will “repay with affliction those who afflict you” and “grant relief to you who are afflicted” when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven (1:6–7). Chapter 2 is the centre: the day cannot have come, because “the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed” (2:3), who sets himself up in God’s place. Something now restrains him; when it is removed he will appear with false signs, deceive those who “refused to love the truth” (2:10), and be destroyed by the Lord Jesus “with the breath of his mouth” (2:8). Paul had taught this in person (2:5), so he writes in shorthand, and some details, above all the restrainer, are now uncertain. This commentary takes the man of lawlessness to be a final individual opponent, while the same lawless spirit works throughout the age, and the restrainer to be most likely God’s providence through government and law. Then Paul gives thanks that God chose and called them, and bids them stand firm (2:13–17). Chapter 3 rests on the faithfulness of God (3:3): Paul asks for prayer, then commands the idle to “earn their own living” (3:12), recalling his rule, “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat” (3:10). The church is to withdraw from the disobedient, yet “warn him as a brother” (3:15).

Where it leads: to Christ. The letter gives the Lord Jesus what the Old Testament gives the LORD. The lost are shut out “from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might” (1:9), echoing Isaiah 2:10; he slays the lawless one as Isaiah’s promised King slays the wicked, “with the breath of his lips” (Isaiah 11:4). The man of lawlessness stands in the line of Daniel’s king who would “exalt himself and magnify himself above every god” (Daniel 11:36): the counterfeit who claims divine honours, undone in a moment by the true Son. Yet the goal of Christ’s coming is not only judgment. He comes “to be glorified in his saints, and to be marveled at among all who have believed” (1:10), and the gathering of his people to him (2:1) belongs to that one coming. Paul prays “that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him” (1:12).

For us. Second Thessalonians guards against two lasting errors: feverish speculation about dates that unsettles the church, and an idleness that leans on others and calls it spirituality. It tells suffering Christians that God sees and will answer, so they need not avenge themselves. It does not explain every detail of the end, but it explains enough: evil runs on God’s timetable and ends at Christ’s coming. Until then the task is plain: pray, stand firm, work quietly, treat the wayward as brothers, and “do not grow weary in doing good” (3:13).

1.title: Relief Is Coming
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens the second letter. Before Paul corrects the false report about the day of the Lord (chapter 2) or the idle (chapter 3), he steadies a suffering church with thanksgiving, with the certainty of God’s justice, and with prayer.

The message. God has not forgotten his persecuted people. Their faith and love, growing under pressure, are his work and the visible sign that he judges rightly. Wrong will not go unanswered: when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven he will repay those who afflict them, give rest to the afflicted, and be glorified in all who believed. Until then God will finish what he has begun in them.

Why it was said. The persecution had grown worse since the first letter (see the introduction), and suffering always raises the question whether God sees, and whether the wrong will ever be put right. A church that had been told the day of the Lord had already come (2:2) needed to hear what that day will really be like, and that it lies ahead.

How the chapter makes its case. The greeting (vv. 1–2) repeats almost word for word the first letter’s: nothing at the foundation has moved. Paul thanks God that their faith and love are overflowing, and boasts of their endurance (vv. 3–4). That endurance is evidence of God’s righteous judgment (v. 5), which will be seen in full when Jesus comes: relief for the afflicted and just punishment for their persecutors (vv. 6–8), eternal ruin away from the Lord’s presence for those who refuse the gospel (v. 9), and glory for Christ in his people (v. 10). So Paul prays that God will make them worthy of his calling and carry every good intention through to the deed (vv. 11–12).

Where it leads. The chapter gives Jesus the place of the LORD of the Old Testament: he comes in the fire of Sinai, with angels at his command, and his face is the presence from which the lost are shut out. Yet the goal of his coming is not fire but glory, his own glory seen “in his saints”, and the astonishment of everyone who believed. The one who will judge is the one who was judged in our place, and the last word of the chapter is grace.

For us. When you suffer for Christ, God has not lost track of you, and you need not settle the score yourself. Hold on, keep loving, pray for those who hurt you, and lift your eyes to the day when Jesus will be marvelled at, and you with all his people will see why it was worth it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before he corrects anything, Paul tells a shaken church that nothing at the foundation has moved: the same three men write, to the same church, held in the same God, with the same grace and peace. The greeting is almost word for word the first letter’s, and the repetition is itself the comfort.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why a Second Letter So Soon

Paul lays the foundation before the correction: grace and peace from God our Father (see the note on vv. 1–2).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church squeezed by hostility and a rumour is first told where it is: in God our Father.

Now: A frightened congregation cannot hear correction until it has been steadied, and what steadies it is truth about God, not a change of mood.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A shaken church is told first where it really lives: in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who still give it grace and peace.

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy. The church is now more harshly persecuted and unsettled by a claim that the day of the Lord has come (see the introduction), yet the greeting is almost word for word what Paul wrote a few months before. The same three men: Paul; Silvanus, the Silas who had been beaten and jailed with Paul at Philippi (Acts 16:19–24); and Timothy (1 Thessalonians 3:2).

In God our Father. One small change is worth catching. The first letter said “in God the Father” (1 Thessalonians 1:1); here it is “in God our Father”, a word that gathers founders and harassed congregation under one fatherhood. And the address says where they are: not in the pressure or the confusion, but in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Paul sets the Father and the Son side by side as the one home of a church, and a Jew raised to say “the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4) would not place a mere man beside God like that. To be in God and in Christ is to be the Father’s children and joined to the Son, so that nothing in Thessalonica or anywhere else can separate you from his love (Romans 8:38–39).

Grace and peace from the Father and the Son. Grace is God’s undeserved favour; peace is what it produces: reconciliation with God, made by the blood of his Son’s cross (Colossians 1:20), and the settled wholeness that flows from it. Both come equally from the Father and the Son, one source named twice. And both are about to be tested: this letter contains flaming fire, a man of lawlessness, a strong delusion, and a congregation told to withdraw from some of its own members. It opens with grace and peace and closes the same way (3:16, 18), and everything hard sits inside that frame.

The one fountain of every blessing. Our Father does not change his greeting when his children are in trouble. He speaks the same grace and peace over the frightened church as over the flourishing one, because neither was ever based on how they were doing. The Father who gave his Son, and the Son who gave himself, stand together at the head of this letter as the one fountain of every blessing, and nothing in the fire or the confusion that follows will reach back far enough to dry it up.

In everyday life. Whatever your workplace, your diagnosis or your quarrel, the most important fact about where you are is this: you are in God.

Why does Paul repeat almost exactly what he wrote before? Because frightened people need to hear that the ground has not shifted. Someone had used Paul’s name to tell them that the end had come and they had missed it (2:2); the quickest way to steady them was to sound exactly like himself. Repetition in Scripture is rarely filler. When God says the same thing twice, his people need it twice, and Christians who have heard the gospel a thousand times still need the thousand-and-first.
verseByVerse.note: Written soon after 1 Thessalonians, probably also from Corinth, to a church still under persecution and now confused about the day of the Lord.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sees his suffering people and will put things right when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven. Paul thanks God for a church whose faith and love are growing under persecution (vv. 3–4), calls their endurance evidence of God’s righteous judgment (v. 5), and describes the day that will bring relief to the afflicted, just punishment to those who refuse the gospel, and glory to Christ in his saints (vv. 6–10). Then he prays toward that day, that God will make them worthy of his calling (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment as Justice

Repayment rests on God's justice, not his temper (v. 6). Because God has undertaken to judge, Christians may never take revenge (see the note on v. 8). On ‘eternal destruction’ and exclusion ‘from the presence of the Lord’, see the note on v. 9 and its box “Where Christians differ: eternal punishment or annihilation?”.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The promise of judgment was given to persecuted people to take revenge out of their hands (see the note on v. 8).

Now: This doctrine is written to make the wronged patient, not to gratify them (see the note on v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is right, because your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing. Therefore we ourselves boast about you in the churches of God for your steadfastness and faith in all your persecutions and in the afflictions that you are enduring.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has made this persecuted church grow in faith and in love for one another, so Paul owes him thanks and tells the other churches how they are standing.

We ought always. A curious way to open a thanksgiving. The word is opheilomen: we owe it, as one owes a debt, because of what God has visibly done. The thanks goes not to the Thessalonians but to God for them. Their growth is his work.

Growing abundantly. Over-growing, the way a vine outruns its trellis (hyperauxanei, found nowhere else in the New Testament). Paul had prayed for exactly this (1 Thessalonians 3:10). God answered.

The love of every one. The second verb means overflowing, running past the brim (pleonazei), the answer to another prayer (1 Thessalonians 3:12). Note “every one”: not the congregation in general, but each person. Persecuted groups often turn on each other; fear makes people suspicious, and suffering makes them short. This one was overflowing outward. God makes frightened, ordinary people stand, and then love one another under the very pressure meant to break them apart.

We ourselves boast. The pronoun is emphatic. Paul, who never sought glory from anyone (1 Thessalonians 2:6), goes round the churches telling them what God is doing in Thessalonica.

Steadfastness and faith. Not their numbers or gifts but their steadfastness, hypomonē, the endurance that stays under a load without putting it down, and their faith, which here includes faithfulness: staying loyal to Christ. We reach for size and visible success; God looks for faithfulness under strain. The persecution itself is not good, and v. 6 says God will repay it. But God uses it as a gardener uses the wind that bends a young tree to drive its roots deeper.

The steadfastness of Christ. Where does a frightened young church get endurance like this? Paul names the source later, praying that the Lord would direct their hearts to the steadfastness of Christ (3:5), the same word. Their endurance is borrowed. Christ stayed under the load laid on him all the way to the cross, and for the joy set before him endured it (Hebrews 12:2). Joined to him, his people endure with his endurance. What Paul boasts of is, at bottom, the Lord Jesus made visible in a persecuted congregation: his patience and faithfulness showing through people who could never have produced them.

Is it right to boast about a church? It depends on what is boasted of and who gets the credit. Paul has just thanked God for this growth; his boasting is the public side of his thanksgiving (compare 1 Corinthians 1:31), and he praises not talent but endurance, the Spirit’s fruit. Such boasting encourages weaker churches, honours God, and tells struggling believers their faithfulness has been seen. What would be wrong is boasting in size, prestige or our own cleverness, or praise that hides the God behind the people.

My faith doesn’t feel as if it is growing. Growth is rarely visible from inside, and often seen first by others. The Thessalonians were frightened and confused, and Paul still saw their faith over-growing. Measure growth not by feelings of strength but by what is still standing: you are still praying, still coming back to Christ, still loving people who are hard to love, still holding on under pressure you did not choose. That holding is growth. And ask God for more, as Paul did for them, because it is his gift before it is your achievement.

verseByVerse.quote: This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are also suffering—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their faithful endurance is a plain sign that God judges rightly: he is fitting them for his kingdom, and he will vindicate them.

Evidence of the righteous judgment. God is not vindicated by the fact that his people are being hurt. What Paul calls evidence (endeigma, a proof, like an exhibit that settles a case in court) is what he has just described: their steadfastness and faith under persecution. Paul told the Philippians the same: their fearlessness was a clear sign of their salvation, “and that from God” (Philippians 1:28). Nobody stands like that over nothing: the righteous Judge is not waiting until the last day to begin; he is already holding his people up, fitting them for glory, writing his evidence into their endurance.

Considered worthy. Counted worthy, judged fit (kataxiōthēnai). It is not merit earned by suffering; Paul will pray that God would make them worthy (v. 11), which he would not need to do if they were achieving it themselves. God declares them fit for the kingdom he is pleased to give (Luke 12:32), and their endurance proves the faith he gave them is real.

For which you are also suffering. They suffer because they belong to God’s kingdom: “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22; 1 Thessalonians 3:3–4). Their affliction is not random misfortune God is making the best of, but the kingdom’s own road. And since God’s judgment is still ahead, the day of the Lord cannot already have come while they are still suffering, which prepares the way for chapter 2.

Suffering, then glory. That road was walked first by their King. “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” the risen Jesus asked (Luke 24:26). Suffering then glory is the shape of his own story, and we are fellow heirs with Christ, “provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him” (Romans 8:17). Walking his road marks them as his. The world reads such pain as evidence that their God is weak or absent. Paul reads it the other way round: a God who was absent would have left them to collapse, and they have not collapsed.

In everyday life. The colleague who freezes you out because you will not join the joke, the relative who sneers at your faith: none of it means God has forgotten you. Do not go looking for suffering, and do not dramatise ordinary friction. But when it comes because of Christ, do not be ashamed.

What about suffering that has nothing to do with my faith, like illness or grief? This verse speaks of suffering for the kingdom, but the wider truth reaches further. God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and the Father uses every trial to refine and train his children (Hebrews 12:5–11; 1 Peter 1:6–7). Your illness is not persecution, and you need not call it that. But the endurance God gives you in it is still his work, still evidence of grace, and still preparing you for the kingdom where there will be no more pain.

Uncertain wording. The Greek has no “this is”: the word “evidence” simply stands beside the previous sentence, so Paul does not say outright what the evidence is. Most take it to be their steadfastness and faith (v. 4); some, the whole situation of suffering and endurance together. The first is the more likely: the sign is their endurance, not the persecution itself.

verseByVerse.quote: since indeed God considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to grant relief to you who are afflicted as well as to us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will repay those who afflict his people and give the afflicted rest, and he will do both when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven.

God considers it just. Paul grounds what follows not in God’s anger but in his justice. Divine judgment is not a loss of temper: a judge who let cruelty pass would not be merciful but unjust. The persecutors’ choices had victims, and the accounting is the work of a good God rather than a provoked one.

Relief. The symmetry is exact: affliction to the afflicters, and to the afflicted, relief. Anesis is a loosening, rest, what happens when a strained rope is let out or a besieged city is relieved. And “as well as to us”: Paul is not an official announcing an outcome from a safe distance, but another man waiting for the same rest.

Revealed from heaven. Relief comes when the Lord Jesus is revealed, and not before. Paul does not promise the persecution will stop; he gives them a date they cannot see and cannot hurry, a harder comfort than deliverance next month and a far more durable one. Apokalypsis is an unveiling: the Lord they already serve, and the justice they cannot now see, will simply become visible, and the whole creation will see that the King was on his throne all along, just in every judgment and kind in every delay.

One coming, not two. At this one unveiling come relief for the church and judgment on its afflicters, together, in public. Paul knows of no earlier, secret coming in which believers are quietly removed before the trouble, which is why this commentary reads the Lord’s return as a single public event, as set out at 1 Thessalonians 4:17. Many faithful Christians read the prophecies differently, and they love the Lord’s appearing as truly as anyone.

With his mighty angels. Literally, the angels of his power (Matthew 25:31). The one who was arrested in a garden, and could have called on more than twelve legions of angels and did not (Matthew 26:53), returns with them at his command.

Is it wrong to want God to punish those who have hurt me? Wanting justice is not wrong: the souls under the altar cry out for it (Revelation 6:10), and so do the psalms. What is wrong is wanting to take it yourself, or wanting the person to be lost rather than repent. A Christian holds both: a longing for wrong to be put right, handed over to God, and a prayer that the one who did it might be converted, as Saul the persecutor was. Leave the verdict to the Judge, and pray for the defendant. The believer who knows God is just is the only person who can afford to be gentle (Romans 12:19–21).

Why does God let persecution go on so long? His patience is giving time for repentance, including the persecutors’ (2 Peter 3:9), and he is doing something in his suffering people that comfort could not do (v. 5). The Thessalonians did not see the end in their lifetimes, and their persecutors may have died unrepaid by any human court. But the delay is not neglect: the date is fixed, and no case is closed until the Judge closes it.

verseByVerse.quote: in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord Jesus himself will carry out God’s just punishment on all who do not know God and do not obey the gospel.

In flaming fire. Fire is the standing Old Testament image for God made visible and for his holy judgment: the burning bush (Exodus 3:2), Sinai wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire (Exodus 19:18), the Ancient of Days whose throne was fiery flames (Daniel 7:9–10). Paul puts Jesus where the God of Sinai stood.

Inflicting vengeance. A word modern readers wince at. Ekdikēsis is just punishment carried out by the one authorised to carry it out, not personal spite. Paul forbids personal revenge flatly, quoting the Lord’s word that vengeance is his (Romans 12:19), and that is the point: it belongs to God, and here Christ himself carries it out. A Christian can be told never to take revenge because God has undertaken to see the matter dealt with.

Who do not know God. Old Testament language for the pagan world (Psalm 79:6; Jeremiah 10:25). Not knowing God, in Scripture, is not innocent ignorance but a refusal of the knowledge that was available (Romans 1:18–21), and each is judged by the light he was given (Romans 2:12).

Who do not obey the gospel. People who have heard the message and refused it. Between them the two phrases cover everyone outside Christ, uninformed and informed, under one verdict. And note the verb: not “believe” but “obey” (compare Romans 10:16). The gospel is not merely an offer to be weighed on its merits. It announces that God has installed his Son as King, and it comes with a command: God “commands all people everywhere to repent” (Acts 17:30). To shrug at it is not neutrality; it is a refusal.

Nothing left for the fire to burn. The fire of Sinai now burns around the Lord Jesus, and it is his right. Yet the same Lord who will command the fire once stood under it in our place, so that everyone who obeys the gospel finds that the fire has already fallen on Christ, and nothing is left for it to burn.

What about people who have never heard the gospel? They are not judged for rejecting a gospel they never heard, but for refusing the God they did know, in creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16). Yet the Bible gives no hope that anyone is saved apart from Christ: there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12), and people call on him only when they hear (Romans 10:13–15). So this verse should send the church to the nations, not into speculation. We leave the hidden judgments to a God who is perfectly just, and we do what he commanded: go and tell.

What does it mean to obey the gospel? To repent of sin and trust Jesus Christ as Saviour and Lord. This is not earning salvation by good works; it is the obedience of faith (Romans 1:5), bowing to the King by receiving him, and from it flows a life of following him, imperfectly and truly. The person who refuses to come has disobeyed the gospel, however politely.

Uncertain wording. Paul repeats the article (“on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey”), so he may mean two groups, pagans who never knew God and those who heard the gospel and refused it, or one group described twice, as in Hebrew parallelism. Both readings are held; either way the verse takes in everyone outside Christ.

parallels.desc: the LORD will come in fire

verseByVerse.quote: They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who refuse the gospel will suffer a ruin that never ends, shut out from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might. This is among the most solemn sentences Paul wrote, and it should be handled without relish.

Eternal destruction. Eternal (aiōnios) is the word used for eternal life; Jesus sets eternal punishment and eternal life side by side (Matthew 25:46). Destruction (olethros) means ruin, the loss of everything good, and does not by itself mean annihilation: in 1 Corinthians 5:5 the man handed over for the destruction of the flesh goes on existing. The ruin is a state, and eternal tells us it is never reversed.

Away from the presence. The clause to weigh. “Presence” is literally face, and the phrase echoes Isaiah 2, where men hide from before the terror of the LORD and the splendour of his majesty. As the ESV reads it, the punishment is an exclusion: shut out from the face of God, the source of all joy, light and life. Hell is not most deeply a chamber of torments but an absence. Every kindness, beauty and ordinary pleasure of a human life came from him, and to be finally away from him is to be away from all of it. Separated from his favour, though not from his justice: God is present in hell in his holiness, and absent in every blessing.

Depart from me. The Lord of this verse is the Lord Jesus of verse 7, and the words of exclusion are his own: depart from me (Matthew 7:23; 25:41). The one who will close the door is the one who wept over the city that would not come to him (Luke 19:41–42), and who said, Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden (Matthew 11:28). Hell is, at its heart, to be finally without Christ, as heaven is to be always with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). No one will be shut out by a stranger; they will be shut out by the Saviour they refused. And the Son who will say those words was himself forsaken on the cross, so that no one who trusts him ever will be. He went outside the presence that he might bring us in.

How a Christian holds this. Paul is not feeding anyone’s appetite for the fate of their enemies. He writes to people being hurt, to tell them the wrong will not stand for ever, and the effect he intends is patience, not satisfaction. God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11), and the man who wrote this had unceasing anguish in his heart for those outside (Romans 9:2–3). Anyone who can state this doctrine without grief has not understood it.

In everyday life. Let this verse give you patience when you are wronged, and courage to speak, kindly and soon, to someone who is drifting from God. And if you fear it describes you, that fear is not the mark of the people in this verse, who do not know God and do not care to; it is a summons to the Saviour who has promised never to cast out anyone who comes.

How can a God of love do this? Love that is not also just is not love but indifference; and the measure of his love is not that there is no judgment, but that he sent his Son to bear it for all who would come (Romans 5:8).

Is endless punishment fair for sins committed in a short life? The weight of a wrong is measured not by how long it took but by whom it was against: striking a stranger and striking a king are not the same act. Sin is committed against the infinitely holy God, who is owed all our love, so it is far heavier than it feels to us. Nor is the punishment the same for all: the one who knew his master’s will and ignored it is judged more severely than the one who did not (Luke 12:47–48). We may not see every reason yet, but the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25).

How can I be happy in heaven if someone I love is lost? Scripture does not give every detail, but God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4), and we will see his justice as clearly as his mercy. For now, let the question propel you: while they live, the door is open.

Where Christians differ: eternal punishment or annihilation? Some (annihilationists or conditionalists, who hold that the lost are finally destroyed and cease to be; among them Edward Fudge, Clark Pinnock and, tentatively, John Stott) argue that eternal destruction means the wicked cease to exist, a destruction whose results are eternal. Universalists say all will eventually be saved. Those who hold these views include believers who love Scripture and argue from it, and the question is what the texts say. This commentary’s view: Eternal destruction is everlasting, conscious ruin: exclusion from God’s gracious presence for ever. The same word “eternal” describes both the punishment of the wicked and the life of the righteous (Matthew 25:46). Scripture speaks of the smoke of their torment rising for ever and ever (Revelation 14:11; 20:10), and of unquenchable fire (Mark 9:43–48). This is the historic Christian teaching (the Westminster Confession 33.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 32.2). It is terrible, and should move believers to tears and to urgent evangelism, as it moved Paul (Romans 9:2–3).

Uncertain wording. “Away from” (apo) can mean separation, shut out from his presence, or source, a destruction that comes from his presence, as in Isaiah 2:10, where people flee “from before the terror of the LORD”. Both are true of that day. Separation, as the ESV has it, is the likely sense, though the echo of Isaiah keeps the terror of his face in view.

parallels.desc: from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty

verseByVerse.quote: when he comes on that day to be glorified in his saints, and to be marveled at among all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Christ comes he will be glorified in his people and marvelled at by all who believed, and the Thessalonians will be among them because they believed the gospel.

To be glorified in his saints. The small word “in” is the whole point. He is glorified in them, not merely by them: his glory will be seen in what he has made of the people he rescued. They are the mirror, not the light. Think who Paul is saying this to: a small, harassed congregation meeting in somebody’s house, despised by their neighbours, with some of their number already buried (1 Thessalonians 4:13). When the Lord Jesus is revealed in flaming fire with his mighty angels, what everyone will be looking at is them, and in them, him. The day that brings ruin to some is the day of his glory in his people.

Marveled at. A strong verb: believers will be astonished at him, overwhelmed with wonder, and the angels, who long to look into these things (1 Peter 1:12), may well share it. The language echoes the psalms, where God is greatly feared in the council of the holy ones (Psalm 89:7). The wonder is not at the saints’ achievement but at what grace did with such material; on that day they will see in full what they now believe without seeing. If you think your own case too ordinary to be worth much, the finished work will stop heaven in its tracks.

Our testimony was believed. The final clause links the cosmic scene to a particular week in Thessalonica. Why will these people be among those in whom Christ is glorified? Because perhaps a year earlier three travelling men said something in their town and they believed it. Their share in that whole blazing day came to them through a testimony spoken and received, which is why Paul will ask them to hold to what they were taught (2:15). A person’s place on the last day turns on the ordinary act of believing the gospel he was told.

In everyday life. Look at the most unremarkable believer in your church, perhaps the one you find hardest to love, and then look in the mirror. Both of you are going to be part of the display of Christ’s glory on the last day. Treat one another accordingly.

Who are the saints? All who have believed: Paul sets the two phrases side by side. Saint means someone set apart for God, and in the New Testament it is the ordinary name for every Christian (1 Corinthians 1:2), not a rank achieved by a few or conferred after death. If you trust Christ, you are one of the saints in whom he will be glorified, not because you are impressive but because he is.

verseByVerse.quote: To this end we always pray for you, that our God may make you worthy of his calling and may fulfill every resolve for good and every work of faith by his power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because that day is coming, Paul prays that God will make them worthy of his calling and carry every good intention through to the deed, so that Jesus is honoured in them and they in him.

We always pray. Having described the day, Paul prays toward it. The coming of Christ is not, for Paul, a subject for charts; it is a reason to pray.

Make you worthy. This settles the question v. 5 raised: the worthiness is asked of God, not earned. The calling is God’s effectual summons, the call that actually brings a person to Christ through the gospel (2:14), and the God who called is the God who completes.

Every resolve for good and every work of faith. The resolve is the inward decision, every desire for goodness God has planted (Philippians 2:13); the work of faith is the thing actually done (1 Thessalonians 1:3). Paul knows how often the resolve dies before it becomes the deed, made on Sunday and gone by Wednesday, and he asks God to carry both through by his power.

Glorified in you, and you in him. The purpose runs both ways. His name means his person and reputation, all that he is. The first half we might expect: his honour seen in his people, as in v. 10. The second is astonishing, and Paul does not pause over it: “and you in him”. Their glory is his own, shared with the people joined to him. They will be raised with bodies like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21), and will be like him, because they will see him as he is (1 John 3:2). They do not become divine. They shine with a borrowed light, as the moon shines with the sun’s.

According to the grace. Not according to their endurance, which Paul has boasted about, but according to grace, from beginning to end.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul doubts they will make it, or that their calling hangs on their effort. He prays because God keeps his called people through means, and prayer is one of them.

In everyday life. Borrow this prayer for the good intentions that never reached Wednesday. When a good desire stirs in you, to forgive, to give, to speak to a neighbour about Christ, treat it as something God may be starting, ask him to finish it, and take the first step today. Christ’s own obedience never stalled between resolve and deed, and it is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), so you may pray over your pile without dread.

If God does it all by his power, what do I do? You do the resolving and the working; God gives the power. Paul prays for their resolve and their work, and both are really theirs. Grace does not make us passive; it makes us able, and the gap between Sunday’s resolution and Wednesday’s action is exactly where you need him.

Uncertain wording. The closing phrase can be read “of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ” (two persons, as the ESV) or “of our God and Lord, Jesus Christ” (one person, calling Jesus God). The Greek allows either, because “Lord” often stands without the article almost like a name. The ESV’s reading is more likely, since Paul regularly names the Father and the Son side by side (v. 2). Either way, a Jew who confessed one God would not name a man as joint source of God’s grace unless the Son shared the Father’s deity.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ:<sup>2</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>3</sup>We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is right, because your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing.<sup>4</sup>Therefore we ourselves boast about you in the churches of God for your steadfastness and faith in all your persecutions and in the afflictions that you are enduring.<sup>5</sup>This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are also suffering—<sup>6</sup>since indeed God considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you,<sup>7</sup>and to grant relief to you who are afflicted as well as to us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels<sup>8</sup>in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus.<sup>9</sup>They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might,<sup>10</sup>when he comes on that day to be glorified in his saints, and to be marveled at among all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed.<sup>11</sup>To this end we always pray for you, that our God may make you worthy of his calling and may fulfill every resolve for good and every work of faith by his power,<sup>12</sup>so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.

keyVerse.quote: when he comes on that day to be glorified in his saints, and to be marveled at among all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed.
keyVerse.note: The chapter speaks of fire and judgment, but this verse tells us what the day of Christ is finally for: his glory, seen in the people he has saved. It turns a persecuted house church into the place where heaven will look on the last day, and it ties that whole day to the ordinary act of believing the gospel you were told.

1.reflection:
Paul thanks God that the love of “every one” of them is increasing under persecution (v. 3). Why does pressure so often make groups turn on one another, and what would it look like for your church to grow more loving under strain?

Verses 6–8 say God considers it just to repay those who afflict his people. How does knowing that God will deal with wrong free a Christian from revenge, and how can we long for justice while still praying for those who hurt us?

Verse 9 describes hell as being shut out “from the presence of the Lord”. Why is this the heart of it? How should this truth shape the way we speak to friends who do not know Christ?

Paul prays that God will fulfil “every resolve for good and every work of faith by his power” (v. 11). What good intention of yours has stalled between resolve and deed, and how might you pray about it this week?

2.title: The Mystery of Lawlessness
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 is the centre of the letter. Chapter 1 promised relief for the persecuted when the Lord Jesus is revealed; now Paul meets the claim that this day had already come and they had missed it.

The message. Do not be shaken: the day of the Lord has not come, and it will not come until the great rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness. Even that final evil is held back for now and runs on God’s timetable, and the Lord Jesus will end it with a breath. Those who refuse to love the truth will be given over to the lie they chose; but God chose you to be saved and called you to share Christ’s glory. So stand firm in what you were taught.

Why it was said. Someone, by a supposed prophecy, a spoken word or a letter that seemed to come from Paul, had told the Thessalonians that the day of the Lord had arrived (see the introduction). To a church promised relief on that day (1:7), still hunted and still burying friends, it meant either that the promise had failed or that they had been passed over.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul gives an argument they can check (vv. 1–5): that day cannot have come, because the rebellion must come first and the man of lawlessness be revealed, the counterfeit who seats himself in God’s place; and they already knew this from his teaching. For now something restrains him, though lawlessness is already secretly at work (vv. 6–7). When he appears, the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the mere appearing of his coming (v. 8). His power and false signs will deceive only those who refused to love the truth, and God will confirm the lie they wanted (vv. 9–12). Then the contrast: God chose and called the Thessalonians through the gospel to obtain Christ’s glory, so they are to hold to the apostles’ teaching (vv. 13–15), and Paul prays that the Father and the Son will comfort and establish their hearts (vv. 16–17).

Where it leads. The lawless one is a dark copy of Christ: he too has a “coming”, a revealing and signs, and he claims God’s seat. But Christ sat down at God’s right hand because his work was finished and the deity was his from eternity, and the counterfeit falls before his breath. The glory the man of lawlessness tries to seize, Christ gives freely to a persecuted church.

For us. This dark chapter was written to make frightened people calm. Do not chase dates or rumours; know what you were taught, love the truth, and be steady in every good work and word. The worst evil still to come is on a leash, and the hand that holds it belongs to the Father who loved you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The day of the Lord has not come, and the Thessalonians need not be shaken: it will not come until the rebellion and the man of lawlessness appear, and even he runs on God’s timetable. Paul reminds them of what he taught in person (vv. 1–5), says that lawlessness is already secretly at work but is held back for now (vv. 6–7), and shows the lawless one destroyed by the Lord Jesus with a breath (v. 8). His counterfeit wonders will deceive only those who refused to love the truth, and God confirms the lie they chose (vv. 9–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Judicial Hardening

God sends the delusion of verse 11 ‘therefore’ because they refused to love the truth (v. 10). It is a judge’s sentence on a refusal that came first (see the notes on vv. 9–10 and vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul’s cure for a panicked church was an argument they could check for themselves (see the note on v. 3).

Now: On names and patterns, see v. 3; on how the build-up ends, see v. 8.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him, we ask you, brothers, not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, either by a spirit or a spoken word, or a letter seeming to be from us, to the effect that the day of the Lord has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let anyone panic you into thinking that the day of the Lord has already come and you have missed it. Paul cures the panic not by telling them to stop thinking about Christ’s coming, but by teaching it properly.

The coming of our Lord. Here is the emergency that produced the letter. Coming is parousia, the word for the state visit of a king to a city, the coming of 1 Thessalonians 4:15, the very teaching that had been twisted.

Our being gathered together. Episynagōgē is the scene of 1 Thessalonians 4:17, the gathering of the elect from the four winds that Jesus promised (Matthew 24:31). In the Greek Paul joins the coming and the gathering under a single “the”, treating them as one event, not two. And the gathering is to him: the hope is not a place or an escape but a Person.

Shaken in mind or alarmed. Shaken (saleuthēnai) is Luke’s word for an earthquake rocking a prison (Acts 16:26); alarmed (throeisthai) is in the present tense, an ongoing state of panic. False teaching about the end knocks a church off its foundations, then keeps it rattled, and “quickly” shows Paul’s grief at how fast a lie moved them.

A spirit, a word, or a letter. A claimed prophecy, a spoken teaching, or a letter perhaps forged in Paul’s name; he does not know which. That is why he signs this one in his own hand, “the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine” (3:17).

The day of the Lord has come. The verb (enestēken) means it has arrived and is now here. Not near, which Paul taught, but here, and they had missed it. They had been promised relief when the Lord was revealed (1:7); if this was the day, and they were still hunted and still burying friends, then either the promise had failed or they had been passed over.

Not one of them will be missing. The coming of our Lord Jesus Christ is not a rumour that can be counterfeited or a date that can slip by unnoticed. When the King comes, no one will need to be told; and when he gathers his people, not one of them will be missing. His promise to come for his own has never once been in danger.

Does this rule out a secret rapture before the tribulation? Pretribulational Christians hold that the church will be taken away before the day of the Lord begins, and the man of lawlessness appear only after it has gone. But Paul treats the coming, the gathering and the day as one event, which will not come until the rebellion and the man of lawlessness appear (v. 3): most naturally, the Thessalonians would still be here to see them. If a secret removal were the next thing on the calendar, this was the moment to say so, and the simplest comfort in the world. He says nothing of the kind. The more likely reading is one public return, at which Christ gathers his people and judges the lawless one (v. 8). Christians who hold the other view are our brothers; but the church should not expect to be spared the last troubles. It should expect to be kept through them.

How should I respond to end-times predictions today? With calm and with your Bible: Paul’s remedy was a return to what they had been taught (see the note on v. 15). When someone announces that recent events prove the end is upon us, or names a date, ask: does Scripture say this, or only the speaker? Does it make me more faithful, or only more anxious? Jesus said no one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36), and every date ever set has been wrong. Be ready every day, and unsettled by no one.

Uncertain wording. “Seeming to be from us” may go with the letter alone, as the ESV takes it, or with all three, a prophecy, a word or a letter claiming Paul’s authority; nor do we know whether the letter was a forgery or a misreading of 1 Thessalonians. Either way, someone was using Paul’s name for a message he never gave.
verseByVerse.note: Someone was claiming — perhaps even by a forged letter — that the day of the Lord had already come.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come, unless the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day of the Lord cannot have come, because two things must happen first: the great rebellion, and the revealing of the man of lawlessness.

Let no one deceive you. Blunt: whatever the channel, whatever the credentials. When Jesus taught about the last things, his first word was a warning against deception (Matthew 24:4–5, 24).

The rebellion comes first. Now Paul’s argument: certain things must happen first, and they plainly have not; therefore the day has not come. Any of them could run it without him. The first event is hē apostasia, “the rebellion”: “the” marks one particular falling away, already expected, which Paul had explained to them (v. 5). It is most likely a great falling away within the professing church, as Jesus foretold, when the love of many will grow cold (Matthew 24:10–12; compare 1 Timothy 4:1): the climax of a defection already at work (v. 7).

The man of lawlessness. Revealed (apokalyphthē) is the word used of Christ’s own appearing in 1:7: he is a deliberate false copy of Christ. Lawlessness (anomia) says what he is: one who sets out to abolish God’s law and to own no authority above himself. He is very probably the figure John calls the antichrist (1 John 2:18).

The son of destruction. A Hebrew idiom: one destined for ruin. The only other person in the New Testament called that is Judas (John 17:12): the last great enemy and the betrayer share a name, and both end where God said they would. Jesus guarded those given to him, and not one was lost but the son of destruction; and he guards them still.

The obedient Son. The lawless one is best understood against the one he counterfeits. Christ is the Son who came into the world saying, “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8; Hebrews 10:5–7). He kept the law his people broke, to the point of death, and his obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). Sin has always been lawlessness (1 John 3:4), and in this last figure human rebellion comes to a head, as human obedience came to a head in Jesus; the rebellion is defection from him. The last days set the lawless man beside the obedient Son, and the end of each is already written.

A caution about names. Nero, Muhammad, Napoleon, Hitler, Stalin: each was named by sincere believers as the man of sin, and each died without being destroyed by the appearing of Christ. That record should make us modest. Paul gives a pattern to recognise, not a name to guess.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s return is delayed indefinitely. Paul gives them not a reason to relax, but a reason not to panic.

In everyday life. Ask what would keep you from falling away if many around you did. Not your upbringing or your friends, which are exactly what shift when a great defection comes. Only Christ’s hold on you, and your hold on him, fed by his word and prayer, will stand. If your faith is mostly borrowed, go to him for yourself now.

Does the great falling away mean true Christians can lose their salvation? No. Those who fall away professed faith without possessing it: “they went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19); and no one will snatch Christ’s sheep out of his hand (John 10:28). The apostasy should make every professing believer examine himself (2 Corinthians 13:5), but the elect are kept by God’s power through faith (1 Peter 1:5; see v. 13). The rebellion sifts the church; it does not defeat the Shepherd. If the warning troubles you, let it send you to Christ rather than into despair: those who fear falling away and run to him are not the ones walking away.

Where Christians differ: who is the man of lawlessness? Interpretations include: a Roman emperor of Paul’s own time; the papacy, as most of the Reformers held (the original Westminster Confession 25.6 named the Pope as antichrist, and the 1689 London Baptist Confession 26.4 does the same); a principle of evil throughout history rather than a person; or a single individual who will appear just before Christ’s return. This commentary’s view: Paul describes a person (“man,” “he”), revealed at a particular time, destroyed at Christ’s coming (v. 8). So the best reading is that he is a final individual, the climactic embodiment of rebellion against God, appearing at the end of the age just before Christ’s return. Yet the mystery of lawlessness is already at work (v. 7), and many antichrists have come (1 John 2:18): throughout history, persons and powers have shown his spirit, including religious systems that claim God’s authority for themselves. The Reformers rightly saw that spirit at work in the abuses of their day. Believers should not speculate about names, but stay faithful and discerning.

Uncertain wording. Apostasia can mean a religious falling away or a political revolt, and the word alone does not settle which; his readers knew (v. 5). The likely meaning is a great defection within the professing church, perhaps joined to the world’s open revolt against God.

Textual note. Many manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “man of sin”, as the ESV notes; the meaning is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: who opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man of lawlessness sets himself against everything people worship and seats himself in God’s place, claiming to be God.

Who opposes and exalts himself. He sets himself against all religion, true and false, so that nothing is left to worship except himself. Paul is drawing on Daniel: the king who “shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god” (Daniel 11:36), first fulfilled in Antiochus Epiphanes, who in 167 BC set up an altar to Zeus in the Jerusalem temple. Behind both stands the boast of the king of Babylon: “I will make myself like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13–14).

He takes his seat. Temple (naos) is the inner sanctuary. And he does not merely enter; he sits, as on a throne.

Proclaiming himself to be God. The original sin taken to its extreme. The serpent’s offer was “you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5); here is a man who accepts the offer publicly and requires everyone else to agree. The Thessalonians did not have to imagine it: the emperor Caligula had ordered his own statue set up in the Jerusalem temple in AD 40, about a decade earlier, and the empire came close to a Jewish war over it before he was assassinated.

Only one has the right to that seat. Scripture knows of one who rightly sat down in the presence of God. After making purification for sins, the Son sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Hebrews 1:3). The priests of the old temple stood daily at their service and never sat; Christ, having offered a single sacrifice for sins for all time, sat down at the right hand of God (Hebrews 10:11–12). The lawless one claims a seat he never earned and a deity he does not have. Christ took his seat because his work was finished and the deity was his from eternity. He did not grasp at equality with God but emptied himself (Philippians 2:6–7), and every knee, including the knee of the man of lawlessness, will bow to him.

The same material, smaller. The passage is not only about a figure at the end. Every self that sets itself above all authority is made of the same material: the tyrant who demands worship, the culture that says nothing is above the self, the church leader who will not be questioned, and the ordinary heart that says, in its own small kingdom, my will be done. In daily life it looks less like a throne than like a man who cannot bear his plans to be interrupted, or a heart that lets its feelings decide what is right; and each small seat taken in God’s place can be handed back to him in a sentence of prayer.

Should we expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem as a sign of the end? No (see the box below), though many who do expect one read these words with real care, and the question does not touch the gospel. Watch instead for a power that sets itself in God’s place and demands what belongs to God alone, especially in the name of religion.

Where Christians differ: which temple? Some take the temple of God to be a rebuilt Jewish temple in Jerusalem, where the antichrist will sit. Others take it as the church, God’s temple in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 3:16; 2 Corinthians 6:16), where false claims to divine authority arise; or as a picture of usurping God’s place. This commentary’s view: The New Testament never predicts a rebuilt temple with divine approval; Christ is the true temple (John 2:19–21). The language most likely draws on Daniel’s imagery to describe the man of lawlessness usurping God’s place and claiming divine honours, perhaps within what claims to be the church. The point is clear whatever the location: he claims to be God. Christians need not look for a rebuilt temple as a sign.

parallels.desc: exalt himself and magnify himself above every god

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul had already taught them all this in person, so they should not have been shaken. He writes in shorthand because they had heard the full lesson.

One side of a conversation. Paul is not introducing new material, and is slightly exasperated to have to remind them. That is why this paragraph hints without explaining: we are reading one side of a conversation whose other half was spoken aloud in a house in Thessalonica. It is why the restrainer is unclear to us and was not to them. The main point is not obscure: the day has not yet come, certain things must happen first, and Christ wins.

The last things for new converts. In a few weeks with brand-new converts out of paganism (Acts 17:2), Paul taught the last things in enough detail to refer to it now in shorthand. He did not regard it as advanced material to be held back.

I have told you beforehand. Paul is doing what his Lord did. Speaking of false christs and false signs, Jesus said, “See, I have told you beforehand” (Matthew 24:25); and in the upper room, “I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe” (John 14:29). Forewarning is how Christ shepherds frightened people. He names the hard things in advance, so that when they come they confirm his word instead of shaking it, and even the darkness of the last days becomes evidence that he knew, and that he is Lord of it.

If some of Paul’s spoken teaching is lost, are we missing something we need? No. God has given us in Scripture everything necessary for his glory and our salvation, faith and life (the Westminster Confession 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6). Paul’s spoken words helped them with details we cannot now recover, but nothing we need for faith and obedience was left out of what God caused to be written. The parts of this chapter that are dark to us are dark at the edges, not at the centre. Hold firmly what is clear, loosely what is uncertain, and let no one fill the gap with a confident guess.

verseByVerse.quote: And you know what is restraining him now so that he may be revealed in his time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work. Only he who now restrains it will do so until he is out of the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lawlessness is already secretly at work, but for now something holds it back, and the lawless one will appear only when God allows, in his time.

What is restraining him now. The most argued-over verses in the letter. Paul’s readers knew what he meant (v. 5); we do not (see the boxes at the end of this note).

Revealed in his time. The lawless one does not choose his own hour. Even the final rebellion runs on a timetable set by the one it rebels against.

The mystery of lawlessness. Paul says it “is already at work”, in the first century. It is a mystery because it is still hidden: what will finally appear openly in one man is operating now, out of sight.

Until he is out of the way. Whatever the restrainer is, evil is plainly being held back for now. Someone has a hand on it.

Weighing the proposals. The Roman state held anarchy back, and Paul calls the governing authority God’s servant (Romans 13:4); this would also explain why he writes so guardedly. The preaching of the gospel to all nations (Matthew 24:14) is a serious suggestion, and Michael (Daniel 12:1) fits the “he” of v. 7. Two proposals fit less well: Paul himself died long ago while the restraint continues; and the Spirit is everywhere, and Scripture nowhere speaks of his being taken from the world.

All authority. Behind every candidate stands God, who alone decides when to lift the restraint, and who has given all authority in heaven and on earth to his risen Son (Matthew 28:18). The church need not identify the restrainer to be at peace; it needs to know who sits above it. Nor does God’s control make him the author of the evil he restrains: he holds it back, judges it, and in the end his Son destroys it.

Evil has been on a leash. The God who said to the sea, “Thus far shall you come, and no farther” (Job 38:11), has drawn the same shoreline around the mystery of lawlessness. It will be revealed only in his time, and let out only to meet the Son who ends it with a breath. Through its whole history evil has been on a leash, and the leash is in our Father’s hand.

In everyday life. Pray for those in authority this week by name (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Their work, however imperfect, is one of the means by which God holds back lawlessness so that the gospel can be preached.

Does “until he is out of the way” mean the church will be taken away first? Dispensational Christians argue so, taking the restrainer to be the Spirit working through the church (see “Weighing the proposals” above and the box below). But the church is not the thing removed. It is the people who will see the lawless one appear and then see him fall.

If evil is being restrained, why is the world still so bad? Because what we see, bad as the news is, is sin under restraint, not at full strength, and that should frighten and comfort us at once. Every law that punishes violence, every conscience that flinches, every government that keeps a basic order, is part of God’s restraining mercy (Romans 13:3–4). The evil that breaks through is real, and God will judge it; but that we can still live, work, marry, worship and raise children is a daily gift of a God who is holding back the flood.

Where Christians differ: who is the restrainer? No one now knows for certain what “restrains” the lawless one; the Thessalonians knew (v. 6), but we do not. Suggestions include: the Roman empire and the rule of law (the most common early church view); the Holy Spirit; the preaching of the gospel; the archangel Michael; or Paul himself. Some dispensationalists (Christians who read history as a series of distinct eras, with separate purposes for Israel and the church) argue that the restrainer is the Holy Spirit in the church, removed at a pre-tribulation rapture. This commentary’s view: The best answer is humility: Paul does not tell us. Most likely he refers to God’s restraining providence, working through the order of government and law (Romans 13:1–4), which holds back the full outbreak of lawlessness until God permits it. Nothing in the passage teaches a secret rapture of the church; Paul never mentions believers being removed here, and the gathering to Christ comes with his visible coming (v. 1).

Uncertain wording. In v. 6 the restrainer is a thing (to katechon, what restrains); in v. 7 a person (ho katechōn, he who restrains). Paul moves between the two without explanation and names neither. What is clear is that the lawless one is now held back until God’s time; what is not is the restrainer’s identity, most likely God’s providence working through government and law.
verseByVerse.note: No one now knows for certain what “restrains” the lawless one; suggestions include the rule of law, the Roman empire, and the preaching of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the lawless one appears, the Lord Jesus will destroy him effortlessly, with a breath, simply by coming.

The breath of his mouth. The Lord does not draw a sword; he exhales. The word is pneuma, breath, the same word as spirit and wind. Paul is quoting Isaiah, where the shoot from the stump of Jesse “shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked” (Isaiah 11:4). John sees the same: from the mouth of the rider on the white horse comes a sharp sword, and the enemies of God fall before it (Revelation 19:15, 21). The voice that said “Let there be light” and “Lazarus, come out” is the voice that ends him.

The appearance of his coming. Appearance means shining forth (epiphaneia), and coming is parousia again. He brings him to nothing simply by arriving, the way darkness is undone when somebody opens a shutter, and the man who claimed to be God is undone by the true God’s appearing.

The proportions are the message. Paul has spent several verses making this figure as alarming as possible, and then disposes of him in half a sentence. That is deliberate. Whatever this power turns out to be, it is not in the same category as the one who ends it. Paul is not giving the church a monster to watch for; he is telling a shaken congregation that the worst thing coming will be dealt with by the Lord Jesus without effort. This is the King we serve: the Word through whom the worlds were made, whose speech is power, whose presence is light, and before whose face every claim to deity falls silent. He has only to come.

In everyday life. Think of the thing that most frightens you: a regime, an ideology, a disease, a person who has power over you. Whatever it is, it is smaller than the breath of Jesus. Pray about it with that size in mind.

Is this the same as the battle of Armageddon? It describes the same reality: the final overthrow of every power opposed to Christ at his return (Revelation 16:14–16; 19:11–21). But in Revelation no fighting is described: the armies gather and are struck down by the sword from Christ’s mouth; Paul’s version has only a breath. Scripture never pictures the end as a long war whose outcome is in doubt, but as rebellion gathering and then collapsing before the King. That one event, the visible coming of Christ, brings the resurrection, the gathering of his people, the destruction of the lawless one and the final judgment together.

parallels.desc: with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked

verseByVerse.quote: The coming of the lawless one is by the activity of Satan with all power and false signs and wonders, and with all wicked deception for those who are perishing, because they refused to love the truth and so be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lawless one will come with Satan’s power and counterfeit wonders, and they will deceive those who are perishing, because they refused to love the truth that would have saved them.

The activity of Satan. Even his arrival is a parousia, the royal-visit word used of Christ. The lawless one has a coming, a revealing, signs and a claim to be God, and behind it the energeia, the active working, of Satan, who has never created anything and can only imitate. He can counterfeit power and copy signs, but he cannot counterfeit the cross, and he cannot make anyone love the truth. Only God does that.

False signs and wonders. Power, signs and wonders: the standard biblical trio for God’s own mighty works, used by Peter of Jesus at Pentecost, “a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs” (Acts 2:22). The lawless one has the same list, in counterfeit: “false” is literally “of the lie”, wonders that, whether or not they are conjuring tricks, point somewhere untrue. Miracles alone do not prove truth. Deuteronomy had already ruled on it: if a prophet gives a sign and it comes to pass, and then says let us go after other gods, do not listen, for the LORD is testing you (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). Jesus said false christs would perform great signs (Matthew 24:24; compare Revelation 13:13–14). The test of a message is never its power. It is its truth.

Wicked deception. He conquers chiefly not by force but by persuasion, and it works on those already on the road to ruin.

They refused to love the truth. Paul explains why the deception works, in a searching sentence. Not that they failed to grasp the truth or found the arguments unconvincing: they refused to love it. The problem lies in what they love, and better evidence does not cure that. This is not a verdict anyone may pass on a particular doubter: honest questions are not the same as refusing to love the truth, and many who now believe once asked them. But most of us know this from the inside: we find it easiest to believe whatever lets us keep what we already love, whether comfort, control or the good opinion of others, and hardest to believe the truth that would cost us them. And the little clause at the end matters: “and so be saved”. Loving the truth was the road out, and it was open. They were not trapped; they declined a rescue, and the next two verses must be read in that light.

What it means to love the truth. We often treat truth as a correct answer on a form. Paul says it is something to love: to welcome it, to want it even when it is unwelcome, and to let it have the last word. Timothy Keller often pointed out, drawing on the English Reformer Thomas Cranmer, that what the heart loves the will chooses, and the mind then supplies the reasons. So the cure for refusing the truth is not first a better argument but a new love, and that is what the gospel gives. The truth Paul means is not a bare idea but Christ, who is “the truth” (John 14:6) and who loved us while we did not want him. Once you know that the truth about you, however hard, is told by someone who died for you, it becomes safe to want it.

In everyday life. Ask God for a love for the truth, and watch where truth costs you something: the passage you avoid because it rebukes you, the fact about yourself you would rather not hear. You see that love when you ask a friend to tell you honestly where you are wrong, and thank him for it; when you would rather be corrected than comfortable.

How can I tell a true work of God from a false one? Not by how impressive it is, but by what it points to and whether it agrees with Scripture. Does it exalt the Christ of the Bible, crucified and risen, as Lord (1 John 4:1–3)? Does the message match what the apostles taught, or add to it (Galatians 1:8)? Does it lead to repentance, holiness and love, or to fascination with the spectacular and the person doing it? A genuine work of God will always send you to Christ and his word; anything that makes you need a new revelation, a special leader or a sign in order to believe is already leading you away.

Can a real Christian be deceived? A believer can be confused or misled for a time, as the Thessalonians were. But a true believer will not finally be carried away into the lie of the lawless one, because God keeps his own and gives them a love for the truth that he does not let die (John 10:27–29). He keeps us not by making deception impossible to meet, but by giving us his word, his Spirit and his church, and by making us love the truth. Stay close to all three.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false, in order that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth but had pleasure in unrighteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because they refused the truth, God gives them over to the lie they wanted, and they will be justly condemned for preferring unrighteousness.

A strong delusion. One of the hardest sentences in Paul, and it should not be softened. God is the subject. Strong delusion is energeia planēs, an active working of error. Everything depends on “therefore”: it follows the refusal of v. 10. God confirms the blindness they chose.

The old pattern. It is Pharaoh, who hardened his own heart, and whose heart God hardened (Exodus 8:15; 9:12); the lying spirit sent to Ahab’s prophets (1 Kings 22:19–23); and Romans 1, where God gave people up to what they had already chosen (Romans 1:24–28). Until then God had in mercy held back the error they wanted; now in justice he lets it loose on them.

What is false. Literally, the lie: that this man is God, the serpent’s lie in the garden in its final form.

Had pleasure in unrighteousness. They enjoyed the alternative (John 3:19–20; on unbelief and what a person loves, see the note on vv. 9–10).

The truth has a face. The truth they did not believe is the gospel of 1:8, and at its centre a Person, who said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), the true light coming into the world (John 1:9). So the final delusion is the end of a long refusal of Christ. And the lie they come to believe, that a man may make himself God, is the exact reverse of the truth they rejected, that God became man to save sinners. Those who would not have the Son who humbled himself are given over to the man who exalts himself.

Pursued when we loved the darkness. God is just in every judgment. But the same God who gives the persistent rebel over to the lie he chose pursued us in his Son when we too loved the darkness, and gave us a love for the truth we did not have. That we see at all is mercy; that we love Christ at all is grace. The difference between the deluded and the saved is not that we were wiser, but that he was kind.

In everyday life. Do not toy with sin. Blindness comes gradually: a sin enjoyed, excused, defended, then a doctrine adjusted to make room for it. If there is a sin you are enjoying, bring it into the light today (1 John 1:9). But if there is a sin you hate and keep falling into, you are not the person these verses describe; the fight against it is itself the Spirit’s work in you (Romans 7:22–25).

Could this describe me? I am afraid I am deluded. Your anxiety is itself evidence against it. The people in these verses do not want the truth and are content; wanting it is the opposite condition, and the beginning of the road out (v. 10). The passage was written not to diagnose our neighbours or wound tender consciences, but to comfort a church wondering how so many could be taken in: God is not absent even from that. If you want Christ, come to him; he has promised never to cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37).

Where Christians differ: does God cause people to believe lies? Some find this incompatible with God’s goodness. This commentary’s view: God is not the author of sin, and he does not deceive the innocent. He sends delusion as a judgment on those who have already refused the truth and loved unrighteousness, giving them over to what they chose. Like the hardening of Pharaoh, it confirms and punishes persistent rebellion (the Westminster Confession 5.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 5.6). The sinner remains fully responsible.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Against that darkness stands God’s choice: the Thessalonians are safe because God chose them and called them to share Christ’s glory. Paul thanks God for choosing and calling them through the gospel (vv. 13–14), tells them to stand firm in the teaching they received from the apostles (v. 15), and prays that the Father and the Son who loved them will comfort and establish their hearts (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, and the Means It Arrives By

Verse 13 puts the whole of salvation into one sentence, and verse 14 ties God’s choice to the means he used, ‘through our gospel’ (see the note on vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: After the lawless one, what Paul asks for is undramatic: stand firm and hold to what you were taught.

Now: Teaching about the last things is meant to produce steadiness in ‘every good work and word’ (v. 17).
