verseByVerse.quote: But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth. To this he called you through our gospel, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unlike those who perish, the Thessalonians are safe, because God chose them to be saved and called them through the gospel to share Christ’s glory.

Brothers beloved by the Lord. A sharp reversal, point for point. Those who perish refused to love the truth; these were chosen. Those were given a delusion; these were sanctified by the Spirit. Those had pleasure in unrighteousness; these believed the truth. And the address: in the first letter he called them loved by God (1 Thessalonians 1:4); here the love is Christ’s. A small shift and a large claim, made without stopping to argue.

God chose you. Here is salvation in one sentence: the Father chooses, the Spirit sanctifies (makes holy), and the Son’s glory is where they are heading. Firstfruits would mean among the first converts in their city and region, the first sheaf of a harvest God would go on reaping (on the other reading, see the textual note below). Either way, the verse teaches election: the initiative was God’s and it came first. Election is God choosing, before the foundation of the world, particular people to be his own and to be saved, moved by his love and by nothing he found in them (Ephesians 1:4–5).

Sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth. God chose the end (salvation) and the means (the Spirit’s work and faith): no one is saved without trusting Christ, and no one who trusts him need wonder whether God chose him.

Through our gospel. Verse 14 anchors it to something they can remember. Election was worked out in history through the preaching of the gospel and the effectual call, God’s inward summons by which the outward message actually brings a person to Christ (1 Corinthians 1:23–24). The eternal choice reached them through three men preaching in their town, the point he made at 1:10 about the testimony that was believed.

The glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. The goal is sharing Christ’s glory (Romans 8:30). Set it beside v. 4: the glory the man of lawlessness tries to seize is given away freely to a persecuted congregation in Macedonia. Not one link in the chain was forged by them, and not one can be broken by the lawless one or the devil behind him.

What kind of election is this? Arminian Christians, brothers who also confess salvation by grace, hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe. But Paul says God chose them to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth: faith and holiness are the means God chose to bring them to salvation, not the reason he chose them. The cause of the choice lies in God, in his love, not in anything foreseen in them.

How can I know I am chosen? Not by looking into God’s secret decree, but at the chain Paul gives: called through the gospel, believing the truth, being made holy by the Spirit. If you have believed the truth and the Spirit is making you holy, you have the marks of God’s choice. You do not climb into heaven to read the book of life; you look at Christ. Election is not a riddle to be solved before you dare to believe. It is a comfort given to those who already believe, to tell them their faith was God’s idea before it was theirs.

If God has chosen, why should we evangelise? Because God chose the means as well as the end. He chose these people to be saved through belief in the truth, called through the gospel. No one believes without hearing, and no one hears without a preacher (Romans 10:14). Election is the reason evangelism succeeds, not the reason to stop. Paul endured everything for the sake of the elect (2 Timothy 2:10). We do not know who they are; we preach to everyone, and God brings his own.

Textual note. “Chose you as the firstfruits” raises a real question about the original wording. The Greek manuscripts divide between aparchēn, firstfruits, and ap’ archēs, from the beginning, and the two look almost identical in the capital letters of the old manuscripts. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV and NKJV, read “chose you from the beginning”, as the ESV notes: from eternity.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So stand firm, and hold on to the apostles’ teaching that you received, whether by word of mouth or by letter.

Stand firm. Stēkete is the soldier holding his position (1 Thessalonians 3:8). Not advance, not work out the timetable: hold the ground you are on.

Hold to the traditions. Traditions (paradoseis) means what has been handed over: here the apostolic teaching, not later church customs.

Spoken word or letter. Paul puts his preaching and his writing on the same level, one of the earliest signs that apostolic writing carried the weight of apostolic speech. The spoken half we no longer have (v. 5); the written half is what we are reading.

The answer to the crisis. They had been shaken by a spirit, a word, or a letter (v. 2). The remedy is to go back to what they were taught, and hold on. A congregation that knows what it was given is very hard to panic.

What was handed over. The traditions have a centre, and Paul names it when he lists what he delivered as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Holding to the traditions is holding to him. The Colossians received Christ Jesus the Lord as one receives a tradition, and are warned against teaching according to human tradition and not according to Christ (Colossians 2:6–8): the line between what the apostles handed on and every later addition: the one hands on Christ, the other hands on men. To stand firm is to keep hold of the Lord who was handed to us.

What it does not mean. Not that all tradition is bad. The creeds and the great Reformation confessions are handed-on treasure, but they stand under Scripture and are to be corrected by it.

What does holding to the traditions look like in practice? Knowing the apostles’ teaching well enough to notice departures from it. Read the New Testament regularly and whole. Learn a good summary of the faith, a catechism or confession, so that the shape of the gospel is fixed in your mind. Sit under preaching that explains the text. When a new teaching arrives, however exciting or authoritative the speaker, ask where it is written. Holding on is not a feeling of conviction; it is a habit of returning, again and again, to the word that was handed to you.

Where Christians differ: Scripture and tradition. The Roman Catholic Church cites this verse to argue that there are two sources of authority: Scripture and unwritten apostolic tradition passed down through the church. Orthodox churches hold a similar view, and both honour the apostles’ teaching deeply. This commentary’s view: Paul’s oral and written teaching had equal authority, because both came from the apostle. But the content of the apostolic tradition is now preserved for us in the written Scriptures. We have no reliable access to other apostolic oral teaching beyond what is written. The apostles’ spoken teaching was the same gospel they wrote down, and Paul himself points the church to what we say in this letter (3:14). So Scripture alone is now the final and sufficient rule of faith, by which all later traditions must be tested (the Westminster Confession 1.6, 10; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6, 10; 2 Timothy 3:16–17).
verseByVerse.note: “Traditions” here means the apostolic teaching handed on to them, whether in person or in writing.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace, comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work and word.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that the Lord Jesus and the Father, who have already loved them and given them lasting comfort and hope, will strengthen their hearts for every good deed and word.

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father. The darkest chapter in the letter ends in prayer. Christ is named first, then the Father, and the verbs that follow are singular, as in 1 Thessalonians 3:11: two persons named, yet they act as one. Paul is not arguing a doctrine; this is simply how he prays.

Who loved us. Before anything is asked, three things are said as already done: he loved us, and gave us eternal comfort and good hope. The love was one decisive act, at a cross outside Jerusalem, and nothing in the future can undo it. Paul asks God not to start loving them but to go on as he has begun. “Eternal comfort” is encouragement that never runs out. Their present comfort had been badly shaken, but the comfort they have been given outlasts the thing shaking it. And good hope is not a wish but a sure expectation of glory, all through grace.

Comfort your hearts and establish them. Comfort (parakaleō) means coming alongside to strengthen, not merely to soothe. “Establish” (stērizō) is the buttressing word, to prop what is leaning, the very thing Timothy had been sent to do (1 Thessalonians 3:2). The Father and the Son, acting as one, hold up what is leaning and steady what is shaken, and they will go on doing it until the day the Son appears and every fear is answered with his face.

Every good work and word. Note where the prayer lands: not in correct opinions about the end times, which is what the chapter has been about, but in what they do and what they say. The outcome Paul prays for is a congregation whose deeds and speech are steady. That is a fair measure of what the doctrine of the last things is for.

In everyday life. Pray this blessing by name for someone anxious about the future, and send them these two verses.

What if I do not feel comforted? The gift and the feeling of it are not the same: your comfort rests on facts, and feelings follow slowly, so pray for it and keep doing the next good work while you wait.

For that day will not come, unless the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction,<sup>4</sup>who opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.<sup>5</sup>Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things?<sup>6</sup>And you know what is restraining him now so that he may be revealed in his time.<sup>7</sup>For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work. Only he who now restrains it will do so until he is out of the way.<sup>8</sup>And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming.<sup>9</sup>The coming of the lawless one is by the activity of Satan with all power and false signs and wonders,<sup>10</sup>and with all wicked deception for those who are perishing, because they refused to love the truth and so be saved.<sup>11</sup>Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false,<sup>12</sup>in order that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth but had pleasure in unrighteousness.<sup>13</sup>But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth.<sup>14</sup>To this he called you through our gospel, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>15</sup>So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter.<sup>16</sup>Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace,<sup>17</sup>comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work and word.

keyVerse.quote: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming.
keyVerse.note: Paul spends several verses making the man of lawlessness as alarming as possible, then disposes of him in half a sentence. The proportions are the message: the worst evil still to come is no match for the Lord Jesus, who ends it without a battle, simply by arriving. That is why a church told about the last rebellion need not be shaken.

2.reflection:
The Thessalonians were “quickly shaken” by a claim about the end (v. 2). What kinds of predictions or rumours unsettle Christians today, and how does Paul’s answer, going back to what they had been taught (vv. 5, 15), help us respond?

The man of lawlessness is a counterfeit of Christ: he exalts himself and takes God’s seat (v. 4). Where do you see smaller versions of that claim in our culture, in churches, or in your own heart, and how does Christ’s self-humbling answer it?

Paul says people are deceived because they “refused to love the truth” (v. 10). What is the difference between agreeing with the truth and loving it? Where does the truth cost you something at present?

Verses 13–14 set God’s choice, the Spirit’s work and our believing side by side. How does knowing that your faith was God’s idea before it was yours steady you when the future looks dark?

3.title: The Lord Is Faithful
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 closes the letter. Having steadied a persecuted church (chapter 1) and corrected the false report that the day of the Lord had come (chapter 2), Paul turns to the ordinary life of a church waiting for that day.

The message. The Lord is faithful, so a church that waits for him can be steady: praying, working and keeping its life in order. A right hope of Christ’s coming does not make people idle; it makes them faithful, busy and orderly. Those who refuse to work and live off others are not to be carried as if all were well, yet they remain brothers, to be warned and won back. Over all of it stand the Lord’s peace and grace, for every one of them.

Why it was said. Some in the church had stopped working, though the first letter had already told them to work with their hands, and were living off others and meddling in their affairs (see the introduction). The faithful were growing tired of carrying them, and the church needed to know how to act without either tolerating the disorder or writing people off.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul begins with prayer and confidence (vv. 1–5). He asks them to pray for the progress of the word, and over against men who do not have faith he sets the Lord who is faithful and will guard them (vv. 2–3). Only then does he command (vv. 6–15). He grounds the command in his own example of working night and day (vv. 7–9) and in the rule he gave from the start, “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat” (v. 10). He calls the idle to quiet work (vv. 11–12), heartens the tired faithful (v. 13), and tells the church to hold back from the disobedient while still warning him as a brother (vv. 14–15). He closes with the Lord’s peace, his own signature against forgery, and grace for all (vv. 16–18).

Where it leads. The faithful Lord of v. 3 is Christ, who stands guard over his people against the evil one, and the closing lines give him what belongs to God: he is “the Lord of peace himself” (v. 16), and his grace is the last word. The chapter’s pattern of life points to him too. The apostle at his workbench followed the carpenter of Nazareth, and a church that warns a wandering brother copies the Lord who went after Peter by the lake. The one who will come in flaming fire meets his disorderly people with grace.

For us. Hope in Christ’s return is meant to make Christians steady, not restless: praying for the gospel’s progress, doing honest work, caring for those who cannot work without paying for those who will not, and correcting one another as family. When doing good wears you down, or someone you love has wandered, rest on the promise the Thessalonians were given: the Lord is faithful.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any hard command, Paul turns the church to prayer and to the Lord’s faithfulness. He asks them to pray that the word will run on and that its messengers will be rescued from their opponents, for not all have faith (vv. 1–2). Over against human faithlessness stands the faithful Lord, who will establish and guard them (v. 3). So Paul’s confidence about them rests in the Lord, and he prays that the Lord will steer their hearts into God’s love and Christ’s endurance (vv. 4–5), the soil in which obedience grows.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faithless, and Faithful

‘Not all have faith’, ‘but the Lord is faithful’ (vv. 2–3): on the reliable Lord who guards his people through trouble, not from it, see the note on v. 3.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul wrote from Corinth (on the ‘wicked and evil men’ of verse 2, see vv. 1–2).

Now: On confidence placed ‘in the Lord about you’, see the note on vv. 4–5.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honored, as happened among you, and that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men. For not all have faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep praying that the message of Christ will run on and be welcomed, and that its messengers will be rescued from those who oppose it, for not everyone believes.

Pray for us. “Finally” (to loipon, as for the rest) marks the closing section, and “pray” is present tense: keep praying. Paul, who prays for them (1:11), asks a harassed young congregation to pray for him. No minister is above needing the prayers of his people.

Speed ahead. Paul asks first not for his safety but for the progress of the message. The verb (trechē) is literally “run”, probably echoing Psalm 147:15, where God’s word “runs swiftly”. It ran from Jerusalem to Antioch, across the sea to Macedonia, through a prison in Philippi and a riot in Thessalonica, and it has never been overtaken.

As happened among you. The second verb (doxazētai) means “be glorified”, as in the prayer of 1:12: the word is glorified when people receive it as God’s word and are changed by it. Then the gracious clause: their own conversion is the pattern of what he asks God to do elsewhere (1 Thessalonians 1:5–6; 2:13). Frightened, confused and harbouring a group who had stopped working, they are still his example of the gospel running well, and writing probably from Corinth, he wanted Corinth to become what Thessalonica had become.

Wicked and evil men. “Wicked” (atopos) is literally “out of place”: perverse, people with whom argument does not work. “Evil” (ponēros) is actively malicious. The Greek has “the” wicked and evil men, which suggests particular opponents, probably in Corinth, where Acts tells of a united attack on Paul and a hearing before Gallio (Acts 18:5–17).

Not all have faith. Paul does not put the hostility down to misunderstanding, as if a better presentation would end it. Faith is not something all could produce if they tried harder; it is God’s gift (Ephesians 2:8), which is why Paul prays. The sentence also prepares v. 3: people are unfaithful, but the Lord is faithful.

I have many in this city. In Corinth the Lord himself spoke to Paul one night in a vision: “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people” (Acts 18:9–10). That is why the word runs: the risen Christ carries it forward. He already called people in Corinth his own before they were converted, and wicked men could not keep his voice from reaching them. Paul asks the church to pray for what the Lord of the harvest has already determined to do, and their prayers become part of how he does it.

In everyday life. Pray this week for one missionary or minister by name: that the word would run through their work, and that they would be protected from those who oppose it.

If God is sovereign, does my prayer actually change anything? Yes, because God has chosen to work through it. He decreed not only the ends but the means, and the prayers of his people are among the means (James 5:16). Paul asked the Thessalonians to pray because their prayers would be part of how God made the gospel run. Sovereignty is not a reason to stop praying; it is the reason prayer is worth anything, for you are asking a God who is able and delights to answer.

When I meet hostility for sharing my faith, have I done it wrong? Not necessarily. Paul met it constantly, and he was not tactless; not all have faith. Sometimes we do handle things badly, and we should be humble enough to ask (Colossians 4:5–6; 1 Peter 3:15–16). But the gospel itself offends, and the most gracious witness in history was crucified. Be gentle, be clear, and leave the result with God.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People fail, but the Lord Jesus does not: he will make you stand firm and keep you safe from the evil one.

The Lord is faithful. Straight after v. 2 comes a wordplay: not all have faith (pistis), but faithful (pistos) is the Lord, with “faithful” first for emphasis. Paul’s answer to human faithlessness is not better people but a reliable Lord. “The Lord” here is Christ, as usually in these letters, and his faithfulness means he keeps his promises and finishes what he begins (1 Thessalonians 5:24; 1 Corinthians 1:9; Philippians 1:6).

He will establish you. “Establish” (stērixei) is the buttressing word, used for the fourth time in these letters (1 Thessalonians 3:2, 13; 2 Thessalonians 2:17) and now made a promise. They had been shaken (2:2), and the promise is aimed exactly there.

Guard you against the evil one. “Guard” (phylaxei) is a sentry’s word. What the Lord’s Prayer asks for, deliverance from evil (Matthew 6:13; John 17:15), here becomes a promise. Satan wants to shake believers loose by persecution, false teaching or disorder. Christ stands sentry over his people in the dark, and the evil one, for all his rage, cannot pluck one of them out of his hand. Paul does not promise they will be spared trouble; he has spent a chapter and a half saying they will not be. He promises they will be guarded through it.

Peter fell, and was not lost. When Satan demanded to sift Simon, Jesus had already prayed that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:31–32); and Peter fell, and was not lost. People fail, churches fail, our own hearts fail us daily, but the faithful Lord’s grip does not depend on ours.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will never be attacked or never stumble, nor does it make us passive: Paul still commands (v. 4) and prays (v. 5). And a believer afraid he might fall away may take this verse as written to him: his safety rests on the Lord’s faithfulness, not on the strength of his fears.

What does an attack of the evil one look like in an ordinary Christian life? Rarely anything dramatic: an accusation that will not let you rest in forgiveness (Revelation 12:10), a doubt pressed at a weak moment, a temptation timed to your tiredness, a quarrel stirred in the church, a lie about God’s goodness whispered in suffering. Resist him, firm in the faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), in the armour God supplies (Ephesians 6:10–18). You do not fight alone: the Lord who guards you has already defeated him at the cross (Colossians 2:15).

Where Christians differ: can a true believer finally fall away? Arminian traditions (which hold that God’s saving grace can finally be resisted) and some Lutheran traditions teach that a genuine believer may lose salvation by turning away; they press the Bible’s warnings seriously, and their concern for holy living is one to share. This commentary’s view: verses like this one ground the Reformed doctrine of perseverance. The promise rests not on our grip on Christ but on his faithfulness: “he will establish you and guard you.” Those whom God has chosen and called (2:13–14) he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:30; 1 Peter 1:5). The warnings are not pointless; they are among the means by which he keeps us. And those who finally fall away show that they were never truly his (1 John 2:19).

Uncertain wording. The Greek (tou ponērou) can mean “the evil one” or simply “evil”, as in the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:13), and translations differ. After chapter 2’s account of Satan’s work (2:9), a personal enemy is the more likely meaning; either way the promise covers both the enemy and everything he does.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have confidence in the Lord about you, that you are doing and will do the things that we command. May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is sure they will obey because his confidence rests on the Lord, and he asks the Lord to steer their hearts into God’s love and Christ’s endurance.

Confidence in the Lord. “We have confidence” (pepoithamen) means we have been persuaded and remain so. Before the hard commands Paul speaks trust, but it is trust “in the Lord about you”, not in their record, which had already wobbled. Confidence of that kind survives disappointment, because it never rested on the people themselves.

The things that we command. “Command” (parangellō), a military and legal word, appears four times in this chapter: not suggestions but the Lord’s commands through his apostle (1 Thessalonians 4:2).

May the Lord direct your hearts. “Direct” (kateuthynai) means clear a road, the verb of 1 Thessalonians 3:11, where the road was Paul’s way back to them; here it is the heart’s way to God’s love. Obedience begins in the heart, and only the Lord can steer it (Proverbs 21:1). The love of God, most likely his love for us (Romans 5:5; Ephesians 3:19), is not a feeling we must work up but an ocean we are led into.

The steadfastness of Christ. “Steadfastness” (hypomonē) is patient endurance, bearing up under a load. This is the right response to chapter 2: not feverish excitement, but staying power. Paul does not tell them to find more of it. He asks God to point their hearts at a man who kept going all the way to a Roman cross (Hebrews 12:2–3). Steadfastness is not produced by gritting our teeth; it is drawn from someone who has already endured, and who now shares his strength with his people as they wait for his return.

In everyday life. Before you correct anyone this week, a child, a colleague, a fellow believer, first tell them honestly what you are confident of in them, and where that confidence rests. Then speak.

How does the Lord direct my heart into his love in practice? Usually through ordinary means, used slowly. He sets his love before you in his word, above all at the cross (Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:10), pours it into your heart by the Spirit (Romans 5:5), and shows it in the Lord’s Supper, in the fellowship of his people and in providences you can trace afterwards. So put yourself where the road is being cleared: read of his love, sing it, pray this verse. When your heart drifts toward fear, resentment or self-pity, ask him to turn it back, and look again at Christ.

Uncertain wording. Both phrases are compressed Greek possessives. “The love of God” could be God’s love for us or ours for him; “the steadfastness of Christ” could be the endurance Christ showed, the endurance he gives, or, as some older translations took it, patient waiting for Christ. Paul’s usage favours God’s love for us and Christ’s own endurance, which he shares with his people; the senses overlap rather than compete.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:6–15 – Idleness, and How to Deal With It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A church waiting for Christ must neither feed idleness nor write off the idle. Paul commands the church to hold back from members who refuse to work (v. 6), points to his own example of working night and day though he had the right to support (vv. 7–9), and repeats the rule he gave from the start: the unwilling are not to be fed (v. 10). He calls the idle busybodies to quiet work (vv. 11–12), urges the faithful not to tire of doing good (v. 13), and shows how to discipline: mark the disobedient and keep apart, yet warn him as a brother (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology:
Discipline That Aims at Restoration

Verses 14 and 15 must be held together (see the note on vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul could command the idle to work because he had worked night and day in front of them, declining support he had every right to (vv. 7–9).

Now: Verse 10 is about the unwilling, not the unable, and it is a rule for the church’s own shared meals and giving.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you keep away from any brother who is walking in idleness and not in accord with the tradition that you received from us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A church member who refuses to work and lives off others, against what the apostles taught, must not be carried along as if nothing were wrong: the church is to hold back from him.

In the name of our Lord. The tone changes sharply. In the first letter Paul asked and urged (1 Thessalonians 4:1); here he commands, by Christ’s authority and as his representative. Something has hardened since he last wrote.

Keep away. “Keep away” (stellesthai) means draw back, hold aloof (2 Corinthians 8:20). It is not excommunication: v. 15 insists he is still a brother. What is withdrawn is the ordinary support and easy fellowship that had been enabling the behaviour. A community that keeps feeding a man who will not work is paying him to stay as he is.

Walking in idleness. “Walking” means a settled way of life, not a single slip. The word for idleness (ataktōs) comes from army life, soldiers breaking ranks (1 Thessalonians 5:14); in context (vv. 7–12) the disorder is refusing to work and living off others (see the note on the wording below).

Not in accord with the tradition. “Tradition” (paradosis) is the word of 2:15. What the apostles handed down included how to live, the duty to work among it (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12): a way of life can depart from their teaching exactly as a doctrine can.

Why they had stopped working. Paul had already told them to work with their hands and to warn the idle (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12; 5:14), but the problem had grown. The false report that the day had come (2:2) may have fed it; the idle may have been living off richer believers, as the poor in Greek and Roman cities lived on a wealthy patron’s gifts (see the introduction); or some may have assumed Christian love meant the church owed them support. Paul’s answer covers all three: work is part of faithful waiting, love does not mean being a burden, and the church must not enable idleness.

The Lord in the midst. When Jesus gave his church authority to deal with a sinning brother, he promised to be among those gathered in his name (Matthew 18:15–20). He stands behind a church that acts in his name, and he is the one doing the correcting. His name is not a weapon to beat the wayward but the authority of one who loves them enough to stop them.

Costly, not bureaucratic. In a small congregation where everyone knew everyone, this meant changing how they treated someone they would see next week: far more costly than any formal process, and the only reason it could work.

What it does not mean. It does not mean shunning those who cannot work because of illness, disability, age or lack of jobs (see the note on v. 10), or cutting off all contact; v. 15 says to warn him, which requires speaking.

What if the person living off others is my own adult child? The principle still applies, with a parent’s tenderness. Love wants the child to flourish, which includes the dignity of responsibility; funding a settled refusal to work, when they are able, pays them to stay where they are. That does not mean throwing them out overnight or withdrawing love, but talking honestly, setting clear expectations and a reasonable timeline, helping them toward work, and letting them feel the consequences of refusing. If illness, depression or addiction lies behind it, get help for that; it is a different situation. Pray, keep speaking, and keep the door of the heart open.

Where Christians differ: how should church discipline be practised? Some churches practise almost no formal discipline; others make it harsh and quick. This commentary’s view: Scripture requires real discipline, carried out by the church under its elders, aimed at restoring the sinner (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5; Galatians 6:1). This passage describes a step short of full exclusion: the person is still a brother (v. 15), but the church withdraws close fellowship to bring him to shame and repentance. Discipline is graded to the offence and its persistence, and always done in love, never as revenge.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “in idleness” (ataktōs) normally means “disorderly” or “out of line”, and some translations render it so. The word alone cannot tell us whether Paul means idleness itself or a wider unruliness; but vv. 7–12 show that the disorder in view is refusing to work and living off others, so “idleness” gives the sense here.
verseByVerse.note: The problem of idleness in the church is now worse than when Paul wrote the first letter.

verseByVerse.quote: For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not idle when we were with you, nor did we eat anyone's bread without paying for it, but with toil and labor we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you. It was not because we do not have that right, but to give you in ourselves an example to imitate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul and his companions had shown the church how to live: they worked hard for their own bread so as to burden no one, though they had every right to be supported.

Imitate us. Before pressing the command, Paul points at himself. Mimeisthai gives us “mimic”, and “you ought” (dei) makes the imitation a duty. “We were not idle” is literally “we did not break ranks” (ouk ētaktēsamen), from the same root as “idleness” in v. 6.

Anyone’s bread. To eat bread is a Hebrew way of saying to get one’s living (Genesis 3:19). Paul lived on no one’s charity in Thessalonica, though the Philippians sent him gifts there (Philippians 4:16).

Toil and labor. Almost word for word the first letter (1 Thessalonians 2:9): tentmaking (Acts 18:3) on top of preaching, a double shift. Kopos is labour to exhaustion, mochthos the grind: Paul is describing being tired. He did not want his support to fall on a poor, persecuted church, or anyone to say he preached for money (1 Thessalonians 2:5–6).

That right. This sentence keeps the passage from becoming a rule that ministers must never be paid. Paul firmly taught that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:4–14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18). He gave up the right voluntarily, here, for a particular reason.

An example to imitate. “Example” (typos) first meant the impression left by a stamp, the word used of the Thessalonians themselves (1 Thessalonians 1:7). Paul made himself a living pattern of honest work, so that no one could claim to be too spiritual for work, and when he tells the idle to work, every reader knows he has already done it in front of them.

Imitators of us and of the Lord. The chain of imitation does not stop at Paul. They had become “imitators of us and of the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 1:6), and he told the Corinthians, “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). Paul’s bench in Thessalonica copied a bench in Nazareth. Jesus was known in his own town simply as “the carpenter” (Mark 6:3): the Lord of glory earned his bread with his hands through the long hidden years. An apostle who would not live at others’ expense was following a Saviour who did not count ordinary work beneath him, and every honest day’s work done in his name bears the impression of his hands.

In everyday life. Someone is watching how a Christian works: whether you finish what you start, whether you complain, whether you cut corners when no one checks. And if you lead others, ask whether you are asking them to do anything you are not doing yourself.

Is my ordinary job really service to Christ? Yes, if it is lawful work done in faith. Paul’s leatherwork was part of his ministry, not a distraction from it, because it adorned the gospel and served his neighbours. The Reformers recovered this: the farmer, the nurse, the mother, the accountant and the cleaner all have a calling from God, not only the minister (Colossians 3:23–24). Your diligence, honesty and cheerfulness at work are worship, and they preach to colleagues who will never enter a church.

verseByVerse.quote: For even when we were with you, we would give you this command: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who are able to work but will not are not to be fed by the church. Its target is the unwilling, not the unable.

We would give you this command. The Greek tense means “we kept giving it”: standing instruction to new converts from the start. He had told them and he had shown them.

If anyone is not willing to work. Among the best-known sentences Paul wrote, and among the most abused. The key word is “willing” (thelei, wants, chooses). The rule targets those who refuse to work, not anyone who cannot find work, cannot do it, or cannot get enough of it: people who had chosen idleness, perhaps for what they took to be spiritual reasons, at the expense of a poor congregation.

Let him not eat. A command, not merely a prediction: the church was not to feed those who could work but would not (Proverbs 10:4). Humanity was made to work (Genesis 2:15); after the fall work became toil but remained a calling, for we bear the image of a God who works. “My Father is working until now, and I am working,” said Jesus (John 5:17). Even our labour is grace: the strength to do it, the bread it brings and the rest that waits at the end of it all come from his hand.

Bread that is worked for. After Jesus fed the five thousand, the crowd came looking for him because they ate their fill of the loaves (John 6:26), and he would not be a mere supplier of free meals: “Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you” (John 6:27). The work God required was to believe in the one he had sent (John 6:29). The one bread that costs us nothing is Christ himself, and it was paid for at the cross. Every other loaf is to be earned, or given in love to those who cannot earn it.

Not a verse against the poor. The distinction between unwilling and unable is not a modern softening; it is what the verse says. Paul organised a great collection for the poor of Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–27; 2 Corinthians 8–9), was eager to remember the poor (Galatians 2:10), and told believers to do good to everyone (Galatians 6:10) and to provide for their households (1 Timothy 5:8). A verse used to justify indifference to the poor is being used against its author.

What the rule protects. Early churches supported the needy generously (Acts 2:44–45; 4:34–35), and generosity can be exploited; the rule protects the church’s charity for those who truly need it. It governs the church’s own shared food and funds, not every question of public welfare, and refusing to subsidise a choice is a different act from abandoning a person (v. 15). Nor does a person’s worth depend on productivity: every human bears God’s image, and the one who finds his whole worth in his job has made the opposite mistake to the idle. Underneath, idleness is a failure of love (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12): the idle man’s food comes from somewhere, and the somewhere is his brothers. The command is not an attack on the poor; it is a defence of them.

The dream of never having to work. Some of us make work a religion, finding our worth in our output (see the note on Luke 12:15–21); others dream of escape: the lottery win, retirement at forty, “quiet quitting”, or the young people in China who began in 2021 to speak of “lying flat”. Both assume that work must be either a saviour or a curse. But in Genesis the man is given work before anything has gone wrong, and the prophets’ world made new is full of it (Isaiah 65:21). The gospel frees us from both mistakes. Your worth is already settled by grace, so work cannot make or break you; and your Lord himself worked, at a bench for years and then on a cross, so no honest work is beneath you. The idle and the overworked are offered the same rest, and then sent back to the bench.

In everyday life. Do today’s work as to the Lord (Colossians 3:23). If you are tempted to coast, remember that someone is carrying what you put down. And when you have coasted, remember that Christ’s work never faltered and is counted as yours (Romans 5:19); return to your own in gratitude, not dread.

How do I apply this when someone asks me for money? Begin with generosity, not suspicion: “Give to the one who begs from you” (Matthew 5:42) is still Christ’s word. But give wisely: where you can, meet real needs, food, a bill paid directly, help finding work, rather than give cash that may feed an addiction. Within the church, let the deacons or leaders who know the situation guide the help, so that the needy are cared for generously and the able but unwilling are lovingly pressed to work. When in doubt, err on the side of mercy, and ask God for wisdom (James 1:5).

verseByVerse.quote: For we hear that some among you walk in idleness, not busy at work, but busybodies. Now such persons we command and encourage in the Lord Jesus Christ to do their work quietly and to earn their own living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some had stopped working and filled their time by meddling in other people’s affairs; Paul calls them, firmly and kindly, to settle down to work and earn their own bread.

Not busy at work, but busybodies. Paul had heard about a group, not the whole church. The English catches a pun in the Greek: mēden ergazomenous alla periergazomenous, not working but working around, doing no business but minding everyone else’s. Idleness is never actually idle: the energy goes into other people’s affairs, gossip, interference, perhaps excitement about the end (1 Timothy 5:13), and in a small community that does real damage, which makes this a church problem, not a private one. Underneath, meddling often feeds a quieter hunger: to matter, to be in the know, to manage other people’s lives when one’s own has been left unmanaged. The first letter had already told them to mind their own affairs (1 Thessalonians 4:11); the advice had not taken.

Command and encourage. “Encourage” (parakaleō) is the word for coming alongside someone to help. Paul does not choose between firmness and warmth, and he does not write the idle off; he calls them back.

Quietly. “With quietness” (meta hēsychias) is the opposite of the restless busyness of v. 11. The cure for meddling is not a rule against gossip; it is a job. The Lord Jesus never meddled and never idled; he did not rush and did not loiter, and he finished everything his Father gave him to do.

Their own living. Literally, “eat their own bread”, as Paul did (v. 8). Self-support frees a person to be generous, so that he “may have something to share with anyone in need” (Ephesians 4:28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian must be in paid employment. Homemaking, caring for family, study and volunteer service are real work. The issue is refusing responsibility and living off others while meddling in their affairs.

Is retirement unbiblical? Not if it is a change of work rather than an end to usefulness. Scripture nowhere commands paid employment to the end of life, but it gives no picture of a long life of self-pleasing leisure either. Retirement can free a believer for prayer, grandchildren, serving the church, hospitality, mentoring younger Christians and volunteer work (Titus 2:3–5; Psalm 92:14). The question is not whether you draw a salary, but whether your time is given to God and others or simply spent on yourself.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay in Greek: not busy at work (ergazomenous) but busybodies (periergazomenous).

verseByVerse.quote: As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the faithful who have kept working, Paul says: do not let others’ idleness wear you down; keep on doing good.

As for you, brothers. “But you” (hymeis de) turns from the idle to the faithful majority who were working and perhaps supporting them.

Do not grow weary. “Grow weary” (enkakēsēte) means lose heart, give up from exhaustion; “doing good” (kalopoiountes) is one compound word, doing what is fine and right. The idleness had a second set of victims: those who had worked all along, carried more than their share and watched others eat at the common table. When disorder is tolerated, the steady giver notices who is not giving, and the reliable one starts to feel like a fool. That slow discouragement can do more lasting damage than the idleness itself, because it works on the people holding everything up.

A hand on the shoulder. Paul does not tell the faithful to police the others; he simply says, keep going. He guards against a swing from naive generosity to cold suspicion, and he speaks to anyone who has been faithful a long time with little to show for it: “in due season we will reap, if we do not give up” (Galatians 6:9).

Consider him. The answer to weariness in doing good is a Person: “Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted” (Hebrews 12:3). Jesus healed lepers who never came back to thank him and washed the feet of the man who would betray him. His goodness was not withdrawn when it was abused, and we, who took far more than we gave, are the proof. No kindness done in his name is lost (Matthew 25:40). He sees what no one else noticed, and one day he will thank his servants himself.

I am exhausted from serving. Does this mean I can never rest? No. Growing weary in doing good means losing heart and giving up, not needing sleep or a holiday. God built rest into creation, and Jesus took his tired disciples away to rest a while (Mark 6:31). Sometimes the faithful thing is to step back from a role for a season, share the load, or say no to a new request. What Paul warns against is the bitterness that says: no one appreciates this, so I will stop caring. Rest your body; guard your heart; the harvest is promised, even when you cannot see it yet.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person, and have nothing to do with him, that he may be ashamed. Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A member who will not obey this letter is to be marked and kept at a distance until he is ashamed, yet always warned as a brother, never treated as an enemy.

What we say in this letter. Paul’s written word carries the same authority as his spoken word (2:15), and the New Testament binds us in the same way.

Take note of that person. “Take note” (sēmeiousthe) means mark, identify: the church is to recognise openly who is persisting in disobedience, rather than letting everyone gossip about it privately.

Have nothing to do with him. The rare word of 1 Corinthians 5:9, 11 (mē synanamignysthai, not mix with): most likely withdrawing table fellowship and close social intimacy, possibly including the Lord’s Supper, so that the person feels the break.

That he may be ashamed. “Ashamed” (entrapē) describes a man brought up short, who suddenly sees how his behaviour looks. Not humiliation for its own sake: in a community where he belongs, that recognition is a mercy, because it is what changes him.

Warn him as a brother. “Warn” (noutheteite) is correction aimed at change. Discipline is family correction, not the expulsion of an enemy: the church stops paying for his idleness and pretending all is well, but it does not stop speaking to him. Everything in the procedure is designed to get him back.

Not an enemy. The church may not treat the disobedient brother as an enemy, because of how God treated the church: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10), and the Son “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). A congregation of former enemies made family cannot write off a brother without forgetting how it got there. Christ’s way with a failing disciple sets the pattern: he warned Peter plainly, let him feel the weight of his denial, then went after him by the lake with the question, “Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). Every withdrawal made in his name is meant to end in a welcome home, and there is always a road home, because he made one at the cross.

The narrow line. Drop the firmness of v. 14 and you get a congregation that tolerates anything and so helps nobody: the person is left as he is, which is not kindness. Drop the warmth of v. 15 and discipline becomes expulsion: an enemy made, a person written off. Behind both halves stands the holiness of the Lord whose name the church bears: a church that shrugs at sin misrepresents him as surely as a church that forgets his mercy.

What it does not mean. It does not license harshness, public shaming for entertainment, or cutting off all contact. Nor should individuals begin discipline on their own; it is the church’s act, led by its elders.

In everyday life. If you must correct a fellow believer, settle before you speak that you want him back more than you want to be proved right. And if you are the one corrected, receive it as a brother’s warning.

What do I do if someone under church discipline is my friend? Stay a friend in Paul’s way: not by pretending nothing has happened or taking his side against the church, but by being one of the voices that calls him back. Do not gossip, or join in easy socialising that tells him all is well; do speak to him, pray for him, and tell him plainly you want him restored. If you think the church has acted wrongly, raise it with the elders, not with him. And be ready to be the first to welcome him when he repents (2 Corinthians 2:7–8).

Where Christians differ: is this the same as excommunication? Some see it as full exclusion from the church; others as a lesser stage. This commentary’s view: it seems to be a step short of full excommunication. In Matthew 18:17 and 1 Corinthians 5:5, 13 the unrepentant person is put outside and treated as an unbeliever; here the offender is still to be warned “as a brother.” Discipline has stages: private warning, warning with witnesses, the church’s withdrawal of close fellowship, and, if repentance never comes, removal from membership. At every stage the goal is restoration (2 Corinthians 2:6–8; Galatians 6:1).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter ends with peace, a signature and grace, and no member is left out. Paul prays that the Lord of peace will give them peace at all times (v. 16), signs in his own hand so that they can tell his letters from forgeries (v. 17), and closes with the grace of the Lord Jesus for them all, the disorderly brothers too (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord of Peace, and a Signature Against Forgery

Only here does Paul write ‘the Lord of peace’, saying of Christ what a Jew would say of God (see the note on v. 16); and his handwritten signature answers the forged letter of 2:2 (see the note on v. 17).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: On what Paul wrote to a year-old, harassed congregation, and how he signed off, see the note on v. 18.

Now: ‘All’, twice in three verses (vv. 16, 18), puts even the disciplined inside the blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in every way. The Lord be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that Christ, the Lord of peace, will give them his peace in every situation and be with every one of them.

The Lord of peace himself. Elsewhere Paul writes “the God of peace” (1 Thessalonians 5:23; Romans 15:33); only here in his letters is it “the Lord of peace”, and “Lord” in these letters usually means Jesus, the giver of peace (John 14:27; Ephesians 2:14). Without stopping to argue it, Paul says of Christ what a Jew would say only of God. “Himself” is emphatic, as at 2:16: peace is not a state they must achieve, through circumstances or a technique for calming down, but a gift he gives.

At all times in every way. “Peace” (eirēnē, Hebrew shalom) is not only calm feelings but wholeness, well-being and right relationship with God and one another. “At all times” excludes no moment, including the ones when the trouble is at its worst; “in every way” means in every form, by whatever means. This church had persecution outside, false teaching within and disorder at the common table. Paul is not describing the absence of trouble; he asks for peace to be given in the middle of it (John 16:33).

The Lord be with you all. One of the oldest and simplest blessings (Ruth 2:4): the greatest gift is the Lord’s presence (Matthew 28:20). And “you all” must include the idle brothers of v. 6 and whoever was to be marked in v. 14. Paul has just told the church to withdraw from them, and he will not close without including them in the blessing: the difference between discipline and rejection, said in one word.

He showed them his hands. The Lord of peace made peace “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20). He slept through the storm and calmed it with a word. He walked into a locked room full of frightened men, said, “Peace be with you,” and showed them his hands. That same Lord is with you all, the faithful and the faltering.

How do I actually receive this peace? By receiving the Lord who gives it: “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). Begin with peace with God through faith in Christ (Romans 5:1), which no circumstance can disturb. Then bring each anxiety to him in prayer with thanksgiving, and his peace will guard your heart (Philippians 4:6–7); fix your mind on what is true about him (Isaiah 26:3). And do not wait for the trouble to end; Paul prayed for peace at all times, which includes now.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “in every place” instead of “in every way”.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine; it is the way I write.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul writes the last lines himself, so that the church can tell his real letters from forgeries like the one that had unsettled them (2:2).

With my own hand. Paul normally dictated his letters to a secretary (Romans 16:22) and took the pen for the last lines (1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11).

The sign of genuineness. “Sign” (sēmeion) means mark, token. This time there is a reason beyond affection: the trouble had started with “a letter seeming to be from us” (2:2). His handwriting authenticates the whole letter, not only the lines he wrote. “In every letter” implies that this was, or would be, his regular practice, and that churches kept and compared his letters: already they carried weight worth counterfeiting.

It is the way I write. Literally, “thus I write”. He answers a forged letter not only with argument (chapter 2) but with a procedure they can use next time; pastors who offer only theology and no practical remedy leave their people defenceless. The written teaching handed down (2:15) had to be protected, and Paul protects it the only way open to him: with his own hand at the bottom of the page.

Whose voice is protected. Paul guards his signature because of whose authority it carries: he was an apostle “not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father” (Galatians 1:1). To forge his letter was to put words in the mouth of the risen Lord who sent him, the Lord who promised that the Spirit would bring to the apostles’ remembrance all that he had said (John 14:26). The hand at the foot of the page is Paul’s, but the voice it protects is Christ’s, which is why the church has always cared which letters are genuine. Every page we open is signed, in the end, by the God who cannot lie.

In everyday life. When a book, a video or a preacher claims to tell you something new from God, ask the Thessalonian question: where is the apostle’s signature on this? If it is not in Scripture, it does not bind your conscience.

How do we know the books in our Bible are genuine and not forgeries? The same way the Thessalonians did, extended over time. The early churches received the apostles’ letters, kept, copied and compared them, and rejected writings that falsely claimed apostolic authority. The New Testament books were recognised by the church, not invented by it: apostolic in origin, agreeing with the apostolic gospel, and received from the beginning. Above all, God’s word bears its own marks, and the Spirit persuades his people that it is his voice (Westminster Confession 1.5; 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.5; John 10:27). The canon is closed: no new writing can join it, and none needs to.

Textual note. Some critical scholars argue that Paul did not write 2 Thessalonians, partly because a forger would protest his authenticity too much. But the stress fits the situation exactly: a forged letter had already caused trouble (2:2). Others point to differences of tone and end-time teaching from 1 Thessalonians, which a changed situation explains well. The early church received the letter as Paul’s without dispute: it is in Marcion’s canon and the Muratorian Fragment, probably echoed by Polycarp and quoted by Irenaeus. The case against Paul is far from compelling, and this commentary receives the letter as his (see the introduction).
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then signed off in his own hand — a safeguard against forgeries such as the one hinted at in 2:2.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter ends where it began, with the grace of the Lord Jesus, and Paul gives it to every one of them, the disorderly included.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Paul began with grace (1:2) and ends with grace, and everything between, persecution, panic, the man of lawlessness, the busybodies, discipline, sits inside that frame. The words are those of 1 Thessalonians 5:28 with “all” added: even those just marked for discipline are inside the blessing, the disorderly whom grace alone can restore.

The note it ends on. Nothing in these three chapters, not the flaming fire, not the eternal destruction, not the withdrawal of fellowship, was written out of hostility; it was written to hold a church together and win its wanderers back. Remember who they were: former pagans and God-fearers from the synagogue in a proud Roman city (Acts 17:4; 1 Thessalonians 1:9), a church perhaps a year old, harassed, confused and quarrelling about who should be working. To such people he wrote about flaming fire, the son of destruction and the glory of the Lord Jesus, and then signed off with the only thing that would get them through the week. Grace, to the whole lot of them, because nothing else would last.

Grace found them in their idols. Grace found the Thessalonians in their idols, kept them under persecution, answered their panic and corrected their disorder. It is the grace of a Lord who will come in flaming fire to be glorified in his saints, and who first came in weakness to be crucified for them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grace ignores sin; the same letter disciplines sin. Grace both forgives and transforms: “the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness” (Titus 2:11–12).

In everyday life. End the day where Paul ended the letter. Whatever went wrong, whatever you failed to do, whatever you still fear about tomorrow, place it inside the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and pray that same grace, by name, over the person in your church you find hardest to love.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honored, as happened among you,<sup>2</sup>and that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men. For not all have faith.<sup>3</sup>But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one.<sup>4</sup>And we have confidence in the Lord about you, that you are doing and will do the things that we command.<sup>5</sup>May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ.<sup>6</sup>Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you keep away from any brother who is walking in idleness and not in accord with the tradition that you received from us.<sup>7</sup>For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not idle when we were with you,<sup>8</sup>nor did we eat anyone's bread without paying for it, but with toil and labor we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you.<sup>9</sup>It was not because we do not have that right, but to give you in ourselves an example to imitate.<sup>10</sup>For even when we were with you, we would give you this command: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.<sup>11</sup>For we hear that some among you walk in idleness, not busy at work, but busybodies.<sup>12</sup>Now such persons we command and encourage in the Lord Jesus Christ to do their work quietly and to earn their own living.<sup>13</sup>As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.<sup>14</sup>If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person, and have nothing to do with him, that he may be ashamed.<sup>15</sup>Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.<sup>16</sup>Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in every way. The Lord be with you all.<sup>17</sup>I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine; it is the way I write.<sup>18</sup>The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.

keyVerse.quote: But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one.
keyVerse.note: Everything else in the chapter rests on this sentence. Set against “not all have faith” (v. 2), it moves the church’s security from people, who fail, to the Lord Jesus, who does not. It is why Paul can ask for prayer with hope, command with confidence, discipline without despair and close with peace.

3.reflection:
Paul asks a young, troubled church to pray for him and for the progress of the word (vv. 1–2), and then reminds them that “the Lord is faithful” (v. 3). How does the Lord’s faithfulness change the way we pray for missionaries, ministers and our own witness, especially when we meet hostility?

Paul worked night and day so as not to be a burden, though he had the right to support (vv. 7–9). What does his example teach about the dignity of ordinary work, and where are you tempted either to coast or to make work your whole worth?

The rule of v. 10 concerns those who are “not willing” to work. How can a church be generous to those who cannot work without paying for those who will not? What would that look like in your church’s care for people in need?

Verses 14–15 hold firmness and warmth together: “have nothing to do with him” and “warn him as a brother”. Which of the two does your church, or do you, find harder, and how does the way Christ treated us when we were his enemies shape the way we correct one another?
